Juno Gemes took these portraits of Quandamooka activist, poet, writer and educator Oodgeroo Noonuccal (1920â€“1993) at home at Moongalba on Minjerribah/North Stradbroke Island. Noonuccal is pictured in the â€˜Black Australia Brisbane 1982â€™ T-shirt she wore when she and her family took part in the protest march before the Commonwealth Games that year.\n\nBorn on Minjerribah, Noonuccal left home to find work in Meanjin/Brisbane in the 1930s and became politically active in the 1940s. She was elected Queensland State Secretary of the Federal Council for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Advancement in 1961 and campaigned successfully for amendments to the Constitution in 1967. Throughout her life, she advocated for cultural pride among First Nations people through her work and gained international acclaim for her writing. Noonuccal returned to Minjerribah in 1971 and established Moongalba, a â€˜sitting down placeâ€™, which she used as an education and cultural centre. There she taught First Nations culture to thousands of schoolchildren on Country. Previously known as Kath Walker, in 1988 she adopted the name â€˜Oodgerooâ€™, meaning paperbark, in protest of the Bicentennial celebrations.

audio.title: Kath Walker part 1
audio.transcript:
I would say that the majority of the Australian people voted Yes in favour of the Aboriginal people merely to clear their guilty conscience. Itâ€™s easy to put a mark on a ballot paper, and I must say this definitely, that there was a small minority group of sincere Australian people but I would say 75 [per cent] of those who voted Yes did it to clear their guilty conscience.

Incidentally, itâ€™s interesting to understand why those terrible discriminative laws were put into the books. In the first place, our civic fathers, or the white manâ€™s civic fathers of long ago, during the â€˜soothing of the dying pillowâ€™ era, the politicians, or the statesmen of that time, were writing over to Queen Victoria saying, â€˜The Aborigine is dying out.â€™ And true, he was â€“ they were poisoning him with strychnine in the waterholes and they were shooting him, and they were doing all sorts of things. And the Aborigine dropped from 300,000 strong to 80,000 in a very short period of time. So it was quite natural for them to say the Aborigine was a dying race.

Now it was during this period of time that the Constitution was being fixed, and as they thought we were a dying race, to save themselves a lot of bother they said, â€˜Well we will not count the Aborigines and we do not have to make laws for the Aborigines, because theyâ€™re going to die out anywayâ€™. And this is the reason today why Aboriginals have not had any education, any decent housing, any facilities that the white Australian enjoys today. Itâ€™s because of that stupid business of thinking the Aboriginals were going to die out.

Mind you, the Aboriginals are a determined lot, and theyâ€™re quite ungrateful. They didnâ€™t die, they lived on and are still living on; in spite of the many attempts to commit genocide and assassinate us all, we are still here. I think weâ€™ll last the white man out, truly.
audio.acknowledgements: This oral history of Kath Walker is from the De Berg Collection in the National Library of Australia. For more information, or to hear full versions of the recordings, visit the National Library of Australia website.

audio.title: Kath Walker part 2
audio.transcript:
In 1965 I think it was, we were invited to go in and talk to the then prime minister, Sir Robert Menzies. There was a deputation from all over Australia of Aboriginal spokesmen and women and we did go in. Sir Robert Menzies had told the public and the politicians, the people of the House, that he would not have a referendum in his lifetime as prime minister. Heâ€™d been badly beaten on the referendum before where he had appealed to the people to outlaw Communism and when the people said â€˜No outlawing of the Communist Partyâ€™, Sir Robert Menzies refused then to have anything to do with referendums in his lifetime as prime minister.

We lobbied the House of Parliament and itâ€™s to their discredit, really, that when we asked them to bring out the laws concerning the Aboriginal people that there was no laws, no books on the Aboriginal people in their archives or libraries, and they had to quickly have them printed, so that the politicians could read what it was, for and against the Aborigines. There was one, however, on the national â€“ the Canberra law book saying that if Aboriginals go into Canberra, any Justice of the Peace could declare them illegal immigrants into Canberra and they could be chased out of Canberra. This still applied to us, incidentally, at this period of time. And we always made a joke of it when we went to Canberra, you know, â€˜If you get into trouble, you know the law on the book. If a JP says Get Out, make sure you get your blanket,â€™ because the law still said that before sending them out of Canberra, they must first issue them with one government blanket. So we were determined weâ€™d get our government blanket if ever they threw us out.  
We told everyone this and we made it a laughingstock â€“ Canberra a laughingstock â€“ to such an extent that the first thing Sir Robert Menzies did was delete that off the Canberra constitution. So itâ€™s no longer there.
audio.acknowledgements: This oral history of Kath Walker is from the De Berg Collection in the National Library of Australia. For more information, or to hear full versions of the recordings, visit the National Library of Australia website.

text.content:
pigment print on paper

Purchased with funds provided by Wayne Williams 2023

Â© Jacob Nash

This portrait of Wiradjuri and Gamillaraay man Beau Dean Riley Smith was taken backstage at Barangaroo, on Gadigal Land, while the dancer was waiting to go on stage for Bangarra Dance Theatreâ€™s performance of _Spirit_ for the 2021 Sydney Festival. Daly River artist and designer Jacob Nash was Head of Design at Bangarra between 2010 and 2023, during which he worked on over 20 productions. Alongside his design work, Nash produced photographs that document the action behind the scenes. While these images appear candid, they carry weight, capturing his subjects in the slip between the stage and the outside world.\n\nRiley Smith is photographed in the paint up room, a sacred space where ochre is applied to the body in intentional designs. Through this process, the dancers become storytellers and are intimately connected to culture. Invited into this space, Nash captures this practice of â€˜transforming from one spirit to anotherâ€™ with respect and reverence. While ochre is the generic term, each region has their own language name for the material. Beneath a hoodie, Riley Smith wears gapan, a white-coloured ochre from North East Arnhem Land. â€˜Itâ€™s always about the magic of the culture and Country,â€™ Nash says. â€˜Gapan canâ€™t be replicated. Itâ€™s just so beautiful in how it dries and how it flakes off into the dust.â€™

gelatin silver photograph on paper

Gift of Robert Rosen 2012

Â© Robert Rosen

In 1993, fashion and society photographer Robert Rosen made this portrait of Nunukul/Noonuccal and Yugambeh brothers Stephen Page AO (b. 1965) and Russell Page (1968â€“2002), as part of a series of black-and-white nude portraits depicting siblings in the arts. Stephen later recalled that he and Russell chose to be painted-up in white ochre for the photograph to represent their shared culture. That same year, together with their brother David Page, Stephen and Russell had established Australiaâ€™s premier First Nations dance company, Bangarra Dance Theatre. Before Russell became a dancer, he was a promising rugby league player. At the age of 16, overcoming an initial rebellion against the discipline of dance, he joined Stephen at the National Aboriginal and Islander Skills Development Association (NAISDA) dance school on Gadigal Land in Sydney and emerged as a breathtakingly original and compelling performer and choreographer. Stephen held the role of artistic director at Bangarra from 1991 to 2022, noting in an interview with _Dance Australia_: â€˜The stories we share are sacred and I feel privileged to play a role in the vital care taking of these stories, through the intimate weaving of culture and contemporary dance.â€™

photographic print from film on paper

Gift of the artist 2021

Â© Ross Honeysett

A YolÅ‹u man of the Mandhalpuyngu language group, actor and dancer David Gulpilil AM (1953â€“2021) was born near Maningrida in Arnhem Land, Northern Territory. In this portrait, Ross Honeysett captures the texture of sand falling through Gulpililâ€™s hands. The image recalls a scene from the 1976 film _Storm Boy_, where Gulpililâ€™s character, Fingerbone Bill, shares the story and dance of the pelican. Gulpililâ€™s palms are opened to the camera, with bright sunlight casting crisp black shadows like a quiet echo.\n\nGulpililâ€™s acting career began at the age of 16 when British director Nicholas Roeg cast him in his film, _Walkabout_, released in 1971. Later that year Gulpilil travelled overseas for the first time to attend the Cannes Film Festival. Over his five-decade career, Gulpilil performed in groundbreaking films and blazed a trail for subsequent generations of First Nations performers and storytellers. As Gulpilil told _This Is Your Life_ in 1979: â€˜I want to share [my culture] to the Western world and Iâ€™m not doing it for myself. Iâ€™m doing it for black and white to know better that we have culture and history still existent.â€™

labels.title: Dialogue
labels.subtitle: Lanatina Iliganoa Ah Kuoi and Sualauvi Ah Kuoi

text.content: This photographic portrait by Lanatina Iliganoa Ah Kuoi and Sualauvi Ah Kuoi, co-founders of the SÄmoan-Australian arts collective House of Iliganoa, emerged from collaborative discussions with fellow artist Kyra Mancktelow during the workshops that shaped this exhibition. In SÄmoa, the making of garments and the act of dressing individuals for celebratory and ceremonial occasions carries deep cultural significance and follows specific rituals and protocols. Through their practice, the House of Iliganoa draw on these cultural traditions to honour the making of the possum-skin cloak led by Mancktelow, and celebrate the many voices that came together through this project.\n\nFor Lanatina and Sualauvi, the stories and histories of First Nations peoples are the foundation of culture and place in Logan and across Australia â€“ what Mancktelow describes as the â€˜first light of Countryâ€™. To express this idea, they have placed Logan-based Waka Waka and Gubbi Gubbi Elder Aunty Faith Green at the centre of the composition, wrapped in the possum-skin cloak. She stands alongside Quandamooka and Yugerra Elder Uncle Gavin Tyson. Surrounding them, in shimmering swirls of light, are members of SÄmoan, Tahitian, Cook Island, Afghan, Tongan, Hmong and MÄori communities. Their movement through the image evokes the journeys and migrations that have shaped Logan into one of Australiaâ€™s most culturally diverse regions.
ink impression on paper\n\nCollection of the artist

For Mancktelow, printmaking is both research and reclamation. The title for this work, â€˜Oc1954.06.386â€™, references the registration number of a Quandamooka dilly bag held in the collection of the British Museum. The museumâ€™s records state that the grass fibre bag was acquired from the Moreton Bay region sometime before 1888. Working from archival images, Mancktelow created a woven copy of the dilly bag. To make this ink impression from the object, she carefully rubbed ink into each woven fibre of the bag before it was laid onto paper for printing. The resulting impression holds the textures, tensions and connections embedded in its making. â€˜Itâ€™s just the way it lands on the paper. The way the string was twined is the way the movement is captured. Any shift will hold the ink â€“ and I canâ€™t take that back. I donâ€™t know what the work will look like until the end.â€™\n\nMancktelow contends with the colonial narratives that exist in archives and museum collections and frame cultural practices as lost, anonymous or disconnected from their culture and Country. In the act of remaking and imprinting the dilly bag, she carries forward knowledge held through enduring connections to maker, place and community.
ink impression on paper\n\nCollection of the artist

****\n\nIn this print, Mancktelow focuses on the relationship between the form and function of a gulayi (Quandamooka dilly bag). Dilly bags have long been made by First Nations peoples across this continent, often woven from natural plant fibres using techniques handed down through generations. They are designed for specific uses, such as gathering food, carrying tools and personal belongings. As Mancktelow explains: â€˜Dilly bags werenâ€™t just small carrying bags; they were made with purpose. They could be woven large enough to carry precious things â€“ whether a child or a skin cloakâ€™; like the possum-skin cloak made for this exhibition. Documenting the detailed design of a woven bag in ink, Mancktelow highlights the importance of cultural knowledge, with the print becoming a record of the skills that foster agency and self-determination within a community. Here the act of making is not just practical, it is closely tied to expressions of identity, responsibility and care.
bronze\n\nCollection of the artist

â€˜Gubagulabuâ€™ translates from Jandai language as â€˜foreverâ€™. This bronze sculpture is part of a series by Mancktelow that reflects on the strength and resilience of First Nations knowledge through the use of both natural fibres and materials introduced after colonisation. Mancktelow recalls visiting the Queensland Museum and studying her Ancestorsâ€™ weavings, including the gulayi (Quandamooka dilly bag). â€˜I was able to trace the technique with my eyes and when I went back home, I just started practising weaving by myself. It felt like I had reawakened something natural within me â€¦ Archival records often describe our practices as lost. But really, some things are just asleep.â€™\n\nFor _Gubagulabu_, Mancktelow first wove a dilly bag using plant fibres with traditional knotting and looping techniques. This woven form was then completely burnt away during the casting process, leaving a bronze replica in its place. Through this transformation, the work becomes a testament to cultural knowledge that may be disrupted but not erased.

labels.title: Bound in story
labels.subtitle: Kyra Mancktelow
labels.medium: possum-skins (legally and ethically sourced from Aotearoa/New Zealand), wax-coated polyester thread, ochre, ash

text.content: possum-skins (legally and ethically sourced from Aotearoa/New Zealand), wax-coated polyester thread, ochre, ash

Made from possum, wallaby or kangaroo skins sewn together with kangaroo sinew and other natural fibres, animal-skin cloaks have been used by First Nations peoples since time immemorial. They are worn for ceremony, warmth and protection, and used as baby carriers, blankets and burial wrappings. Each cloak is unique, with designs on the underside of the skin carrying the story of the wearer and mapping their connection to family and Country. Today, the resurgence of possum-skin cloak making reflects the continuity, strength and resilience of First Nations cultures and identity.\n\nOver the course of the exhibitionâ€™s presentation at Logan Art Gallery, Kyra Mancktelow led the making of this possum-skin cloak through workshops and yarning circles involving Elders and community members from a range of cultural backgrounds. This collaborative process created a space for sharing stories, knowledge and culture, and informed the designs incised into the cloak by Mancktelow. The bold flowing patterns represent the broader Logan community, while smaller circular forms symbolise campsites and gathering places â€“ individual people and cultural groups coming together through the yarning circles. Curling possum tails coloured with ochre from Quandamooka Country reach across the centre of the design, evoking the movement and flow of the Logan River. For Mancktelow, the cloak reflects the way shared histories and experiences enrich connection through â€˜understanding, listening and acknowledgingâ€™.
Indian ink, paper

Each person in Logan carries a constellation of stories shaped by family, culture, migration, education, faith and lived experience. During the presentation of this exhibition at Logan Art Gallery, a group of community leaders and creatives gathered to reflect on the histories, values and experiences that shape their lives and their connections to place and community. Traces of their stories and these conversations were recorded in ink on sheets of paper, gradually accumulating over time. At the end of the exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery, these marked pages will be bound together as a book, stitched with the same thread used to make the possum-skin cloak.

type C photograph on paper

Collection: National Portrait Gallery Purchased 1999

Â© Michel Lawrence

In the late 1970s, photographer Michel Lawrence took a series of portraits of Naarm/Melbourne-based performers, including the band The Boys Next Door. Pictured here are the original members Philip Calvert (b. 1958), Mick Harvey (b. 1958), Nick Cave AO (b. 1957) and Tracy Pew (1957â€“1986). Their first single â€˜These Boots are Made for Walkingâ€™ was released in 1978 and the album _Door Door_ appeared the following year when Rowland S. Howard joined the band. With the issue of their 1980 album _The Birthday Party_, some copies of which were released with the name of the band omitted, The Boys Next Door morphed into The Birthday Party. In 1980 the band moved to London, where they proved enormously influential on the British rock scene. Cave and Harvey went on to form The Bad Seeds, who have garnered critical praise and cultivated popular adulation over several decades.\n\nIn this portrait we see the origin of what would become Caveâ€™s signature look â€“ a slim, tailored suit, reflecting his transition from the chaos of his punky youth to becoming a master of his craft: â€˜I always wear a suit, because I have important work to do and Iâ€™m not going to go to work in a pair of bermudas and bright flip-flops.â€™

gelatin silver photograph on paper

Collection: National Portrait Gallery Purchased 1999

Â© Harry Borden

Michael Hutchence (1960â€“1997) was the charismatic lead singer of the band INXS. The band sold over 50 million records worldwide with hit songs like â€˜Never tear us apartâ€™ and â€˜Need you tonightâ€™ etched in Australian music history. Formed in Sydney in 1977, INXS released 10 studio albums and were the only Australian group to participate in the historic Live Aid concert held simultaneously in London and Philadelphia in 1985. By 1988, INXS were arguably the most successful Australian band ever, with their sixth album _Kick_ selling around 7.5 million worldwide. Hutchence died by misadventure in the Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Double Bay, Sydney in November 1997. Earlier that year Harry Borden took a series of portraits of Hutchence in Paris to promote his last album with the band, _Elegantly Wasted_. During a television interview, the besuited Hutchence stepped out for a cigarette break and Borden leaned over the hotel balcony to capture this infamous shot.

audio.title: Polly Borland on Michael Hutchence
audio.transcript: Iâ€™d known Michael when I was younger. And Iâ€™d done, actually, with Richard Lowenstein and INXS music video. You know, and it was the song that I think broke them in America, _What You Need_. But when I went it to do the photo of him it was really in the dark. Paula was there, they were living together with all her kids in a house in West London. There was something about the whole situation that didnâ€™t feel quite right. You know, they were sort of under siege, you know there was all that kind of press, really awful kind of attention that the English press are very good at doing. Also they were in the bitter battle with Bob Geldof, and he was quite vocal about that. I mean later I found out kind of what was going on, and the way he talked about it, he felt like he was embattled.\n\nI think that photoâ€™s really good. I donâ€™t know why I would put it as one of my favourites but in a way itâ€™s a really powerful photo and I think it alsoâ€™s almost like a prediction. I mean he was extraordinary as a performer, as a talent and he was extremely charismatic, I mean, he was incredible. You know in a way thereâ€™s a kind of a Christ-like feeling to that photo, you know itâ€™s almost like he was the sacrificial lamb or something â€˜cos I think there was a real purity and naivety to Michael, and he was really a nice person. But he was kind of exploited I really feel. Itâ€™s sort of a sad photo and itâ€™s quite hard, that photo, thereâ€™s something quite gritty about it. But yeah, he was a beautiful person. A beautiful person that shouldnâ€™t have ended up dead when he did.

video.title: Michael Hutchence by Harry Borden
video.transcript:
**Harry Borden**: Okay. This is Harry Borden. Iâ€™m making noises on my camera to give the impression Iâ€™m a photographer.

As a portrait photographer Iâ€™m sort of running around a meadow of celebrities sort of trying to capture these kind of people in my butterfly net. I steadfastly adhere to the ethos that a portrait is a record of the relationship you have with a person, and kind of authenticity is really important.

Michael Hutchence was kind of unusual in that respect, in that he I think was kind of very much an incredible kind of frontman. He had this kind of incredible kind of grace, and he did have this amazing sort of charisma. I had a sort of a formal session with him, and the rest of the time was just hanging around. That picture was actually taken during the hanging around time. He sort of nonchalantly kind of came out, and strolled around, and smoked his cigarette. I took a couple of pictures that were generally kind of reportage, and I was sort of hanging over the side of the balcony, and I was just instinctively just snapping.

Heâ€™s not really engaging with the camera at all. Heâ€™s sort of somewhere else. Thatâ€™s the way he was. I mean, we went downstairs and we sort of walked around the Champs Elysees and with all the traffic, and he was sort of pretending to hitchhike.

Itâ€™s a bit harsh to say that he failed. Sort of failure would be based on the assumption that he took his own life, but I donâ€™t think you can blame someone for a tragic accident, which is what I think it was.

It has a lightness of touch, and is genuinely kind of not merely a contrivance, just a sort of a genuine moment.

Purchased with funds provided by Wayne Williams 2018

Singer-songwriter Steve Kilbey (b. 1954) is the frontman of the Australian band The Church and has been its primary member for over 45 years and 27 albums. Formed by Kilbey with Peter Koppes and Nick Ward in the late 1970s, The Church broke through internationally a decade later with â€˜Under the Milky Wayâ€™. Consistently rated among the best Australian songs of all time, the track won them the ARIA for best song of 1988 and was used in the cult film _Donnie Darko_ in 2001. Kilbey has released many solo albums including the 2023 concept album _The Hypnogogue_. He is also a visual artist, whose work expresses his longstanding interest in mysticism and spiritualism.\n\nThis portrait of Kilbey was captured by Gary Ede in 1981, the year the photographer also took the inner-sleeve photographs for The Churchâ€™s debut album _Of Skins and Heart_. In his songwriting, Kilbey prefers to keep the meanings of his lyrics ambiguous. The surprising inclusion of a stiff, fake fish in this portrait playfully echoes that sentiment.

inkjet print on paper

Purchased with funds provided by Wayne Williams 2018

Â© Gary Ede

Gary Edeâ€™s photograph of The Saints, taken in London, shows the bandâ€™s 1978 iteration: Ed Kuepper (b. 1955), Alasdair â€˜Algyâ€™ Ward (1959â€“2023), Ivor Hay (b. 1956) and Chris Bailey (1956â€“2022). Arguably one of Australiaâ€™s most influential punk rock bands, The Saints were formative members of the international punk rock scene. As Kuepper put it, â€˜we had this sound that was totally our own, and we were despised by everybody.â€™ Their first single â€˜(Iâ€™m) Strandedâ€™ was released and distributed on the bandâ€™s own label in September 1976. The band were promptly signed by EMI for a three-record deal, and thus earned the distinction of releasing a punk song before the Sex Pistols did (their single â€˜Anarchy in the UKâ€™ was released in November 1976). In contrast to the typical punk attire of rips and safety pins, The Saints rebelled by wearing button-down shirts and blazers.

Sherbet was one of the most successful Australian rock bands of the 1970s. They began playing at Jonathanâ€™s Disco in Sydneyâ€™s Ultimo where they were spotted by the young Australian talent manager Roger Davies, who would later manage Tina Turner and Janet Jackson. By January 1972, the lineup had settled to the members shown in this photograph: Daryl Braithwaite (b. 1949), Clive Shakespeare (1947â€“2012), Garth Porter (b. 1948), Alan Sandow (b. 1952) and Tony Mitchell (b. 1951). Sherbet was the first domestic act to sell a million dollarsâ€™ worth of records in Australia.

Lewis Morley photographed Sherbet in their birthday suits for the racy _POL_ magazine in 1972. Stripped of their clothes but not their charisma, this photograph exudes their cheeky pop swagger. Morleyâ€™s individual photographs of the band members, also in the collection of the National Portrait Gallery, were used on the cover for the 1975 re-issue of Sherbetâ€™s debut album, _Time Change:_ _A Natural Progression_, first released in 1972.

oil and synthetic polymer paint on canvas

Gift of the artist 2009. Donated through the Australian Government's Cultural Gifts Program.

Â© Ken Done

Founded by designers Anna Plunkett and Luke Sales in 2005, Romance Was Born is an Australian fashion house who produce vibrant and exquisitely crafted attire. Their collections are often produced in collaboration with visual artists and designers such as Del Kathryn Barton, Jenny Kee and, in this instance, Ken Done. Their Done Zone__ 2023 resort wear collection celebrated the bold detail and exuberance of Doneâ€™s paintings. As Plunkett and Sales observed: â€˜The initial splash of inspiration for the collection came from Ken Doneâ€™s reef paintings, sprinkled with the effervescent flavour and spunky attitude of his iconic clothing line.â€™ This suit, a cornerstone of the collection, was hand-painted by the artist himself and the paintbrushes he used are tucked into its pocket. It is flanked by Doneâ€™s 1992 painting _Me_. The artist described this self portrait as showing the two sides of himself â€“ his optimistic, smiling public face and his more pensive, sensitive self. Viewed together, the suit and the painting testify to the way we craft and project shifting personas to those around us through visual codes.

audio.title: Ken Done
audio.transcript:
A self portrait of the artist Ken Done created in 1992. Oil and synthetic polymer paint on canvas measures 102 centimetres high and 76 centimetres wide.

The frame is painted a matte black with a floral and leaf design loosely scratched into the surface. The inner border of the frame is a darkened gold.

The background and figure are a patchwork of clashing colours and patterns. The surface is heavily textured, with brush marks evident and some short hairs from the paint brush caught in the paint. Ken Doneâ€™s face fills the frame; the top of his head, edges of his ears and base of neck, reach the outer edges of the canvas.

A line of thick black paint arcs across the top of his head. His face is divided into shapes, with his forehead painted red with yellow dots on the left side and cobalt blue on the right side, with a stylised white outline of the Sydney Harbour Bridge floating on top. The rest of his face is painted in zones of pink, forest green and blues. A patch of black with yellow stripes features under the left eye. A simplified outline of the Sydney Opera House is painted in white, filled in with blue on the right cheek.

He has painted himself with three non-matching eyes; the left eye, pink and blue with a yellow pupil, the right eye, yellow with a black pupil and a central eye, blue with a yellow pupil outlined in yellow. He has merged a profile face with a full-face representation, reminiscent of a cubist style of painting. Thick yellow paint outlines the yellow eye, eyebrow and side profile of a nose and mouth with a flash of white teeth. This profile sits on top of the right side of the full-face view. The frontal representation is more dominant with the eyes rimmed in black, a black moustache and exaggerated red banana-shaped smile. His neck brings together strong brush strokes of purple, orange, red, black and blue. 

The top half of the background is painted a cobalt blue with the word â€˜meâ€™ painted in yellow block letters in the top left corner. The lower section of the canvas is coloured orange on the left side of his neck and has sections of mottled tones of turquoise, burgundy and green and a patch of yellow with irregular red dots on the right.  
The artist initials, â€˜KDâ€™ are roughly painted in red in the lower right-hand corner. 

Audio description written by Alana Sivell and voiced by Molly Desmond.

video.title: Ken Done
video.transcript:
- I like to make pictures. I've made a few sculptures, I've made a little bit of pottery, but basically I'm a painter. I'm not complaining, but I've had to overcome a lot of early success in the sense that the early things that people saw were very commercial things. I was 40 when I had my first exhibition. It's quite old, really. But, that's just the way it was for me.

If you like visual things, you know, that's what you like, you like all kinds of things and the only criteria should be, was it any good? You know, do you like it? I am very Sydney. I live beside Sydney Harbour which is a fantastic place to be. I kayak on the harbour, I feed the fish, I don't like to catch them anymore. I feed them, in fact, if anybody comes down here and they say, is there any fish around? I say, oh, no, there's no fish around here. No fish around here. But of course there are, top of the tide, there's eight big bream, I almost know them by name, come around each morning. There's parts of the harbour close by here, where we live, that hasn't changed forever. No houses, look exactly the same as when aboriginal people lived here or even later when Captain Cook came through. That's one of the great things about Sydney, I think, is that they've still preserved that natural landscape in some parts. Such a beautiful place. Almost inevitably you'll make pictures that try to be beautiful. You can't be as beautiful as itself, you can never be as beautiful as nature, you can not. But all you can do is to use that environment to lead you to make a painting that somehow might have the feeling of it.

It's a complicated picture and it clearly set out to show that there's a kind of public face that I have. That's most of the time smiling and most of the time optimistic. But there's another face, maybe another even two faces within there that I hope shows a sadder side or a different kind of sensitivity. Glenn designed a house for us. We've known him a long time, he's a lovely man. And I did make a small drawing, but I wanted to make the painting as simple and as elegant as one of his buildings. I love the fact that in the portrait gallery, you've sometimes shown them both together and it just shows his elegant simplicity against the kind of complication of my self portrait which, you know, I would say straight to the psychiatrist, looking at that painting.

00:03:02.097 --> 00:03:05.120
you've sometimes shown them both together

60
00:03:05.120 --> 00:03:07.603
and it just shows

61
00:03:07.603 --> 00:03:10.425
his elegant simplicity

62
00:03:10.425 --> 00:03:14.415
against the kind of complication of my self portrait

63
00:03:14.415 --> 00:03:17.121
which, you know, I would say straight to the psychiatrist,

64

looking at that painting.

65

text.content: synthetic polymer on textile

Founded by designers Anna Plunkett and Luke Sales in 2005, Romance Was Born is an Australian fashion house who produce vibrant and exquisitely crafted attire. Their collections are often produced in collaboration with visual artists and designers such as Del Kathryn Barton, Jenny Kee and, in this instance, Ken Done. Their Done Zone__ 2023 resort wear collection celebrated the bold detail and exuberance of Doneâ€™s paintings. As Plunkett and Sales observed: â€˜The initial splash of inspiration for the collection came from Ken Doneâ€™s reef paintings, sprinkled with the effervescent flavour and spunky attitude of his iconic clothing line.â€™ This suit, a cornerstone of the collection, was hand-painted by the artist himself and the paintbrushes he used are tucked into its pocket. It is flanked by Doneâ€™s 1992 painting _Me_. The artist described this self portrait as showing the two sides of himself â€“ his optimistic, smiling public face and his more pensive, sensitive self. Viewed together, the suit and the painting testify to the way we craft and project shifting personas to those around us through visual codes.

type C photograph on paper

Collection: National Portrait Gallery Purchased 2005

Â© Karin Catt

Newcastle-born photographer Karin Catt took her first celebrity portrait, of INXS lead singer Michael Hutchence performing at the local workersâ€™ club, at the age of 12. She has since photographed many famous faces including these three Australian/New Zealand actors who have all made it big in Hollywood: Guy Pearce (b. 1967), Russell Crowe (b. 1964) and Nicole Kidman AC (b. 1967). Cattâ€™s portraits are taken on her Hasselblad camera, whose square format and sharp lens allow her to compose very symmetrical images. Here, each of her sitters wears a sleek suit, perhaps to project the image of a serious thespian on the rise. Sitting for Catt, Crowe observed, â€˜one of the principal requirements of a portrait photographer has to be communication skills, not only through the lens, but a simple ability to make the subject feel at ease in what may well be an unusual environment. Karin has the gift of getting her subjects to drop their armour and be available to the camera as themselvesâ€™.

labels.title: Johnny O'Keefe "A little bit louder now..."
labels.subtitle: Ivan Durrant

text.content:
synthetic polymer paint on board

Commissioned with funds provided by L Gordon Darling AC CMG 1999

Â© Ivan Durrant/Copyright Agency, 2024

Johnny Oâ€™Keefe (1935â€“1978) was Australiaâ€™s first rock â€™nâ€™ roll star. At a time when radio stations were reluctant to promote local talent, Oâ€™Keefe was the first Australian rock performer to score a chart hit with the 1958 song â€˜Wild Oneâ€™. A raw and exuberant performer, Oâ€™Keefeâ€™s signature tune was â€˜Shoutâ€™, which contained the oft-repeated words â€˜a little bit louder nowâ€™. In 1959 he presided over the television show _Six Oâ€™Clock Rock_ and he was later host of _The Johnny Oâ€™Keefe Show_. Despite Oâ€™Keefeâ€™s success, his personal life was tumultuous. Drug abuse, drinking and overwork contributed to his death from a heart attack at 43.\n\nArtist Ivan Durrant was about 13 years old when he first saw Oâ€™Keefe on television. At the time Durrant had a â€˜rockerâ€™ hairdo and fancied that he resembled Oâ€™Keefe. When he was commissioned by the National Portrait Gallery to create this portrait, Durrant chose to paint the singer as he imagined him at the beginning of his career â€“ an innocent young boy just entering the world of rock â€˜nâ€™ roll.

inkjet print on paper

Gift of the artist 2006

Â© Robin Sellick

Bert Newton AM MBE (1938â€“2021) was one of Australiaâ€™s best-known media personalities with a career spanning seven decades. Often referred to as the â€˜kingâ€™ of television, he was famous for his quick wit and ability to ad lib. In the earliest years of TV, Newton made his debut as straight-guy to Graham Kennedy on _In Melbourne Tonight_ and later as the sidekick to Don Lane on _The Don Lane Show_, who gave him his tenacious nickname â€˜Moonfaceâ€™. From 1976 to 1985 he presented the talent show New Faces, and in 1992 he moved into daytime television with _Good Morning Australia_. His acclaimed musical theatre performances include _Beauty and the Beast_, _The Producers_ and _The Rocky Horror Show_. Newton hosted the Logie Awards 19 times and won the Gold Logie himself four times. Throughout his career he was always immaculately presented in a well-cut suit, such as the one he wears in this photograph taken by Robin Sellick in the Channel Nine studios in Naarm/Melbourne.

gelatin silver photograph on paper

Collection: National Portrait Gallery Purchased 1999

Â© Jacqueline Mitelman

Christina Stead (1902â€“1983) is regarded as one of Australiaâ€™s finest novelists. Stead left Sydney for London in 1928 seeking to escape what she experienced as the stifling parochialism of Australia, as she later expressed in her semi-autobiographical novel _For Love Alone_ (1944). In London, Stead embarked on a successful literary career with _The Salzburg Tales_, a collection of short stories, and her first novel _Seven Poor Men of Sydney_, both published in 1934. Her fourth novel _The Man Who Loved Children_ (1940), said to be based on her own dysfunctional family, gained wide critical acclaim. After over 40 years living in England, Europe and the USA she returned to Australia in 1974 and that year was the inaugural recipient of the Patrick White Award for literature.\n\nJacqueline Mitelman photographed Stead looking sophisticated in a tweed suit. Combined with her direct gaze, the resulting portrait is imbued with a sense of seriousness and intellectual authority.

audio.title: Christina Stead
audio.transcript:
I start with a character, somebody who strikes me very forcibly, and I think to myself, â€˜This is it, this is the oneâ€™. Then I allow life to grow up around that person. I donâ€™t question them. I see how it is with them in life, as you would if you were studying a tree and its background and its ecology. Thatâ€™s kind of a job. And then the drama that arises, arises from them and their relations with their friends, their backgrounds. By the time Iâ€™m finished, it isnâ€™t just one person, naturally, itâ€™s a whole sector, group of people. But in one sense thereâ€™s a hero but sometimes itâ€™s what they call, I think very foolishly, an anti-hero. But I donâ€™t like that expression.

When Iâ€™m fairly advanced with conceiving the character and Iâ€™m beginning to see the lines of force and so forth round the character, I do in fact make many, perhaps five, and perhaps even 20 plans, schemes of all kinds of things, of relations, of deeds and so forth. This is just to organise my mind; I never use them. As I say, Iâ€™m struck by somebody in real life, and this is where I get my characters, in real life. And also itâ€™s not possible to get them anywhere else.

The important thing to me in writing is writing. I love writing, and I used to find myself as a child and a young girl, trying out words, â€˜Thatâ€™s not really blue, the sky, itâ€™s something elseâ€™ and â€˜How would I say that about the leaf?â€™ and so on. These were just trial runs, of course. I wasnâ€™t intending to write when I did this.

This sounds rather a strange thing to say â€“ but I think what inspires me in writing is perfection. I like to get the perfection of an idea or an expression. Naturally one falls short, but thatâ€™s the idea.

I begin with a person who impresses me very much and in quite an animal way, because it begins at once like a love at first sight, itâ€™s exactly like that. And when you love a person at first sight you know nothing about them, you donâ€™t know their intellectual standing. You may vaguely see their personal characteristics, but you really donâ€™t know.
audio.acknowledgements: This oral history of Christina Stead is from the De Berg Collection in the National Library of Australia. For more information, or to hear full versions of the recordings, visit the National Library of Australia website.

video.title: Jacqueline Mitelman
video.transcript:
- I remember when I was very young and still a teenager and doing some work in a darkroom. It was really the first time time disappeared for me. You know, I was so excited about doing it. I think that you have to regard it as a collaboration. Even people who are really well known and photographed all the time feel a bit vulnerable. It's incredibly easy to take a horrible picture of somebody where they look really tense and they don't look like themselves. So I guess I'm interested in people being comfortable.

I don't have any format. I don't have a particular way they have to sit or what is their background. I really have to push it a bit to include a bit of background or include more of the body because that's interesting, but if I had what I wanted I probably would just have like that, you know. Because the eyes are obviously necessary. I'm interested in the eyes, try to get some sort of straight gaze, where at least you have the impression that you're contacting the essence of that person. There was a phrase that I quite used to like, which is Buddha nature, which means you know like that in you which doesn't change. You can take pictures of quite small children, and you know that there's something in that photograph that if you came back, 50 years later, there would be still the same thing in it. And that's sort of, I guess, what I'm interested in.

I mean one of the guides that I have used, it's something that's only really formed in the last probably 15 years, is the different-sidedness of faces, in that, I would ask people, just as a guide, whether they're left-handed or right-handed. Because people who are right-handed, somehow, look to me, better from that right side. The other side, if people are left-handed they generally look better from the left side. Whatever better means. Most people are asymmetrical. There's some very rare people who are symmetrical, but most of us are really quite different.

Taking photographs is a bit like a temporary infatuation, for me, because, I'm not interested in taking awkward pictures of somebody, so it's a bit like, you know that process when you fall in love with somebody, they do one thing and to that one thing you attach all these qualities, which they don't have. They just do that one thing. But you don't want to show somehow, you don't want to see the bad things at state, you just put all the good things together. I've taken photographs of people where I've looked at them afterwards and I've thought, yes, the person who's in love with him sees him like that.

text.content:
gelatin silver photograph on paper

Gift of Richard Woldendorp AM 2017

Â© Richard Woldendorp

Artist Kathleen Oâ€™Connor (1876â€“1968) made her name as an impressionist painter in early 20th-century Paris. Born in Aotearoa/New Zealand in 1876, she migrated to Western Australia at the age of 15. In 1906 Oâ€™Connor moved to Paris where she lived and worked for the next 50 years. A regular exhibitor at the Salon dâ€™Automne and the Salon des Independents, Oâ€™Connor often wrote articles on Parisian art and fashion for Australian newspapers such as _Town Talk_, and fiercely believed that art is â€˜universal, eternal and not parochialâ€™. In 1948, Paris was in a dilapidated state after the Second World War and Oâ€™Connor was forced to return to Australia. In this photograph by Richard Woldendorp, she retains an air of aloof elegance with her two-piece suit and stacks of tortoiseshell bracelets.

type C photograph on paper

Gift of the artists 2003

Â© Montalbetti & Campbell

Songwriter and guitarist Tim Rogers (b. 1969) is best known as the front man of You Am I, a band he formed with his brother Jaimme Rogers and Nick Tischler in 1989. By 1993, when the band released their first album _Sound As Ever_, the other two members had quit and were replaced by Andy Kent and Russell Hopkinson. The album won the ARIA Award for Best Alternative Release, as did their second album _Hi Fi Way_ in 1995. Their third album _Hourly_, _Daily_ debuted at number one and won six awards, including Best Album, at the ARIAs in 1996. You Am I have since consolidated their reputation as one of Australiaâ€™s most successful alt rock bands. The band released their 11th studio album _The Lives Of Others_ in 2020.\n\nCanadian duo Montalbetti + Campbell took the photographs of the band that appeared as the cover art for their album _Sound As Ever_ and made this studio portrait of Rogers two years later. Rogersâ€™ vest, assembled from interwoven organic matter and studded with chillies, is an unexpected contrast to his tailored jacket, perhaps reflecting the hybridity of the bandâ€™s music, which combines a heavy guitar sound with melodic elements and thoughtful lyrics.

synthetic polymer paint on board

Purchased with funds provided by the Basil Bressler Bequest 2001

Â© Bruce Armstrong

Award-winning author Peter Carey AO (b. 1943) is one of only five people to have won the prestigious Booker Prize twice, with _Oscar and Lucinda_ (1988) and _True History of the Kelly Gang_ (2000). This painting was completed after only one meeting between artist and subject. Bruce Armstrong made sketches and photographs of Carey on a visit to New York, where the author was Distinguished Professor and Director of the MFA Creative Writing program at Hunter College. Armstrong returned to Australia to work on the painting on a property on the land of the Dja Dja Wurrung and Taungurung peoples near Kyneton, Victoria, which he was leasing at the time. It was there, on the fringes of â€˜Kelly Countryâ€™, which featured in Careyâ€™s 2000 novel, that the setting for the portrait evolved. Carey is presented in the dry landscape, but he wears an incongruous outfit that would be more at home in New York, situating him as an international intellectual.

oil on canvas

Gift of Robyn Archer AO 2012. Donated through the Australian Government's Cultural Gifts Program.

Â© George Gittoes/Copyright Agency, 2024

Performer, writer and director Robyn Archer AO (b. 1948) became a star with her cabaret stage shows _Kold Komfort Kaffee_ (1978), _The Conquest of Carmen Miranda_ (1978) and _Tonight: Lola Blau_ (1979). Her hit one-woman show _A Star is Torn_ (1979â€“83) toured Australia and ran for a year in Londonâ€™s West End. In the 1990s she began her distinguished career as artistic director of various festivals including the Adelaide and Melbourne festivals. Internationally renowned for her interpretations of classic European cabaret, she won the Helpmann Award for Best Cabaret Performer in 2013. Archerâ€™s 11th album _Classic Cabaret Rarities_ was released in 2021.\n\nGeorge Gittoesâ€™ portrait of Archer in a hot pink suit jacket references her cabaret performances and the inspiration provided by the political satire of Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill, who used the suit as a prop to strip away realism and symbolically highlight the inequities of capitalism and class.

gelatin silver photograph on paper

Collection: National Portrait Gallery Purchased 2012

Â© Estate of Francis Reiss

Barrister Ron Castan AM QC (1939â€“1999) played a leading role in some of Australiaâ€™s most significant litigation involving the rights of First Nations peoples. Senior counsel on the Mabo Land Rights case, he worked with Eddie Mabo for a decade to shape the landmark High Court decision delivered in 1992. Castan was also involved in the development of and amendments to the resulting legislation, the _Native Title Act_, and helped to draft the 1996 Wik case. His Russian Jewish heritage influenced his deep commitment to human rights, social justice and legal reform, and he was a leader in the Jewish community.\n\nFrancis Reiss has captured Castan reclining, somewhat uncomfortably in his suit, on a Le Corbusier chaise lounge in his Naarm/Melbourne office, at ease but not off the job.

type C photograph on paper

Gift of the artist 2004

Â© Estate of Penny Tweedie

Shahleena Musk is a Larrakia woman from Darwin and the Northern Territoryâ€™s Childrenâ€™s Commissioner. Musk is dedicated to community informed law practice, with decades of experience in policy for youth justice. The first Aboriginal student to graduate with a degree in law at Charles Darwin University, Musk advanced to become Crown Prosecutor for the Director of Public Prosecutions in both the Northern Territory and Western Australia. In 2013 she was instrumental in the creation of the North Australian Aboriginal Justice Agency youth team. As a director at the Larrakia Development Corporation she contributed to the #RaiseTheAge Campaign that advocates for raising the age of criminal responsibility in Australia from 10 to at least 14. In this portrait by Penny Tweedie, Musk carries the traditional black robe and wig of a Crown Prosecutor.
Gift of Mark Tedeschi AM KC 2025\n\nÂ© Lewis Morley Archive LLC

This portrait depicts barrister Mark Tedeschi AM KC (b. 1952), the longest-serving Crown Prosecutor and Senior Crown Prosecutor in New South Wales. It was taken by his friend, the photographer Lewis Morley, who used theatrical high-contrast lighting and props to convey the sense of drama that occurs within the courtroom. Tedeschi grasps a king chess piece, while cupping his chin as he contemplates his next move. The chess piece is a visual pun, creating a playful parallel between the litigation battles that take place in the courtroom and the skirmish that takes place on a chessboard. While we can only barely see his robes, Tedeschiâ€™s wig situates him in the lexicon of the law.

gelatin silver photograph on paper

Gift of Patrick Corrigan AM 2004. Donated through the Australian Government's Cultural Gifts Program.

Â© Gregory Weight/Copyright Agency, 2024

Wenten Rubuntja AM (1923â€“2005), an Arrernte law man, worked across a variety of pastoral jobs and was renowned as a sharp-dressing, daring cowboy and jockey at the Hermannsburg Races before he began painting and became involved in advocacy. Summarising the trajectory of his life, he said that when he saw the great artist Albert Namatjira at work, 'Me been forget about stock work â€“ I been sit down with the painting now, till I get to now. For reconciliation and all the organisations, Land Council, Congress, Legal Aid and all that one.' In 1975, Charles Perkins and Rubuntja became chair and deputy chair respectively of the new Central Aboriginal Land Council. Rubuntja was its subsequent chair, and in 1988 he and Yunupingu AM (1948-2023) presented Prime Minister Bob Hawke with the Barunga Statement, calling for a treaty. His paintings â€“ in both 'Namatjira style' and Papunya dot style, depending on their themes â€“ are held in the National Gallery of Australia, the Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory and many other collections.\n\nRubuntja's life story is told in the strikingly original co-written autobiographical history _The Town Grew Up Dancing: The Life and Art of Wenten Rubuntja_ (2002). Photographer Greg Weight travelled with Rubuntja to take a series of images for the book. This photograph was taken at Akepelye (Jessie Gap), a significant ancestral site associated with the Caterpillar Dreaming.
pigment print on paper

Bidjara artist Michael Cook uses the medium of photography to explore his First Nations identity. Typically working in series, Cook coaxes out ambiguous and ultimately open-ended narratives interrogating Australian history. His influential 2014 Majority Rule series of seven photographs addresses the lack of representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in the worlds of business, politics and the judicial system by envisioning a world where First Nations Australians are the majority. Cookâ€™s replication of the same besuited man asserts a sense of strength in numbers and challenges the dominance of those in control. From afar these scenes could be from real life, until we notice the duplication. The repetition is unnerving and uncanny, a sense only amplified by the washed-out tonality of the prints.

oil on canvas

Commissioned with funds donated by BHP Billiton Limited, Rio Tinto Aboriginal Fund, Newmont Australia Limited, Reconciliation Australia, Hon Paul Keating and Hon Fred Chaney 2006

Â© Commonwealth of Australia

Dr Lowitja Oâ€™Donoghue AC CBE DSG (1932â€“2024), a Yankunytjatjara woman, dedicated her lifeâ€™s work to advancing the rights and wellbeing of First Nations peoples. The first Aboriginal woman to complete nursing training at the Royal Adelaide Hospital, she travelled to remote communities, learning about her heritage through â€˜just doing what I could to heal peopleâ€™. Among her many achievements, Oâ€™Donoghue was chair of the National Aboriginal Conference, the Aboriginal Development Commission and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission, where she helped to draft the Mabo legislation.\n\nFor her portrait by Robert Hannaford, Oâ€™Donoghue chose the red suit that she often wore for official occasions, along with jewellery signifying her strength and status as a recognised leader and proud Yankunytjatjara woman.

audio.title: Lowitja Oâ€™Donoghue
audio.transcript:
Iâ€™d never heard of Robert and Iâ€™m not sure that he knew much about me either. But I quickly got to know him and respect him, and I knew that by the questioning and so on that he was really trying to find out more about me. So, Iâ€™m not sure that he knew much about [the] Stolen Generation. After I saw the portrait come out, I myself felt the portrait wasnâ€™t like me because Robert had told me very early in the piece that I wasnâ€™t to smile. He doesnâ€™t like smiling portraits. People who know me of course know that I do smile a lot.

The suit that I wore on the day, I think he was a bit surprised because it was really quite formal and itâ€™s a suit that I wear when I receive the many awards that Iâ€™ve received over the years. My family had no difficulty at all seeing me turn up in that same suit. And because it was a portrait, I thought, well, you know, Iâ€™m an Aboriginal woman and Iâ€™m going to wear the Aboriginal flag, and Iâ€™m going to wear everything red, black and yellow.

Iâ€™m much more proud of the fact that Iâ€™m a nurse and that I was able to use my nursing experience to actually travel to remote areas in my own, well in my own right, just doing what I could to heal people. I didnâ€™t know my people very well and so on, this is one way of getting to know them out on the APY lands. I have had a lot of senior jobs, met just so many people in high places, really. And I enjoyed seeing them but they werenâ€™t the most important things in my life. It was really about making a difference.
audio.acknowledgements: This recording was made during interviews for the National Portrait Gallery's [_Portrait Stories_][1] series.\n\n [1]: /stories

audio.title: Lowitja O'Donoghue
audio.transcript:
This portrait is of Lowitja O'Donoghue, Yankunjatjara woman and Indigenous rights campaigner. It was painted by Robert Hannaford in 2006 in oil on canvas. The work measures about 1.4 m tall by 1.4 m wide, set in its wide frame of dark wood. The portrait is painted realistically with loosely applied brushstrokes. Lowitja wears a bright red skirt-suit and is seated in front of a dark background.

The scene is lit from the top left. Lowitja is illuminated in a soft pool of light filling the top right and centre of the painting. Pale green-grey and blue-grey brush strokes at the top right curve around and down towards the bottom left, their direction changing, sweeping around and getting darker towards the lower edge of the canvas.

Lowitja sits on a dark wood chair in the centre of the image. The rounded corners of its back rise above each of her shoulders. Her head is tilted slightly down to her left with her chin angled up. Lowitjaâ€™s silvery hair is short, parted on the side, and styled in a wave over her forehead. Her skin is in warm honey tones and her cheeks are tinged pink. Lowitja has fine steeply-arched eyebrows above her dark eyes that gaze directly at us. Her nose is broad and deep grooves flow from it to the outer edges of her thin rosy lips. Her lips are closed and slightly downturned, creating soft jowels which frame her broad chin.

In the portrait Lowitja wears a loosley-fitted long jacket that runs down her lap to her knees. It has an Aboriginal Flag pin on the left lapel and is open, with three large round gold buttons gleaming brightly down its left side. A strand of black red and yellow beads and an oval shaped Aboriginal Flag pendant on a fine chain stand out against her black round-necked top.

Lowitjaâ€™s elbows rest lightly on the carved wooden arms of the chair and her hands lie with fingers extended in her lap. On the ring finger of her left hand she wears a wide yellow-gold band, while on her right a ring is set with a large black rectangular stone.

Lowitjaâ€™s red skirt extends over her knees and out of frame. The same red has been used by the artist to sign â€˜Hannaford 06â€™ on the bottom right of the canvas.

Audio description written by Lucinda Shawcross and voiced by Amy Middleby

video.title: Lowitja O'Donoghue and Robert Hannaford
video.transcript:
Robert: I painted Lowitja in my Adelaide studio in West Hindmarsh, and that was a wonderful experience too because Lowitja is so down to Earth, such a lovely person.

Lowitja: It was a surprise to me to be asked to sat with. I'd never heard of Robert, but I quickly got to know him and respect him, and I knew that by the questioning and so on that he was really trying to find out more about me. He went on asking questions, of course, about where I came from, where I grew up, and the whole story of being from ... what is the term? I don't use the term very much, but the term of being from the stolen generation. I was removed as a child, a two-year-old girl, into a children's home up in the Flinders Ranges. That children's home was called Colebrook Home for Half-Caste Children. I didn't like it, of course, particularly when we were told we went in there that our culture was of the devil. Because I heard that too many times I became quite rebellious, because I was always asking the question about; who am I, where did I come from, who's my mother and who's my father, and where are they? Never got any answers to any of that at all.

Robert: When I was painting Lowitja, that was how she sat, that was the truth of what I was... and pictorially, and the expressions on her face. If Lowitja was sitting there smiling that would be a less interesting portrait by a long way.

Lowitja: I, myself, felt the portrait wasn't like me. The reason for that is because Robert had told me very early in the piece that I wasn't to smile. He doesn't like smiling portraits. Now, people who know me, of course, know that I do smile a lot, but I did choose the suit because it was a portrait I thought, "Well, I'm an Aboriginal woman, and I'm going to wear everything red, black, and yellow." It's a suit that wear on a regular basis when I receive the many awards that I received over the years. My family have no difficulty at all seeing me turn up in that same suit. I'd trained at the Royal Adelaide Hospital here, but I had to ... Mater wouldn't accept me for five years, and I was the first Aboriginal woman who was accepted to the Royal Adelaide Hospital. I think I'm more proud of having ... the fact that it took so long for me to be accepted in the first place. I was able to use my nursing experience to actually travel to remote areas and remembering that I was removed, I didn't know my people very well, and so on. This one way of getting to know them out on the lands, just doing what I could to heal people.Â

Poet, journalist and social reformer Dame Mary Gilmore DBE (1865â€“1962) was the first female member of the Australian Workersâ€™ Union. From 1908 to 1931 she championed a variety of causes as editor of the womenâ€™s page of the Australian Worker. In 1930 she published The Wild Swan, a book of verse decrying the destructive effects of colonisation on the land and First Nations culture. In this portrait by Lyall Trindall, painted at the time Gilmore was assembling the poems in her 1939 book Battlefields, the artist has depicted his sitter as strong and determined. In recognition of Gilmoreâ€™s campaigns for social and economic reforms, she was given a state funeral in Sydney, is featured on the Australian $10 note and the Canberra suburb Gilmore is named after her.

audio.title: Mary Gilmore
audio.transcript:
Everybody, here I am, Mary Gilmore, asked to talk to you about Australia, my recollections. Of course, I go such a long way back, 95 years and now nearly going on for 96. Iâ€™ve seen the beginnings. I began myself with a slush lamp, went onto the tallow candle, then to the imported stearin candle, and then to kerosene lamps and from kerosene to gas, from gas to the electric light and now we have ahead of us the atomic to cover every mortal thing that we can think of. It seems an astounding thing for one personâ€™s recollections.

I remember the poor old convicts, so many of them â€“ they worked for my father, some of them. Some of them had backs that were ridged and ridged from the lash. I remember one station owner, a big rich man, and it was noted by his men that when they would go in swimming heâ€™d sit on the bank and he wouldnâ€™t go in. And one day without thinking, the poor man pulled his shirt off and jumped in. Father was in the water, so he caught hold of his arm and said, â€˜Come on, weâ€™ll go race to a different placeâ€™, and he took him right away from where the men could see him. His back was ridged too. And that was how the land was begun, how it was settled in the beginning, how the big Australia with its wide range of international linkings now, began. And those were the people who began it.

Well, we have the Blacks for our background for stories and we have the convicts. In later years, when my book _The Passionate Heart_ was published, I wrote a piece of verse for it on that subject, because I was full of indignation at the idiocy of letting go in silence what was our basic history, and I still feel that way. Itâ€™s called _Old Botany Bay_.

Oodgeroo Noonuccal (1920â€“1993) is a Quandamooka activist, poet and educator. Born on Minjerribah/North Stradbroke Island, she enlisted in the Army in 1942 before committing to political work. Noonuccal was elected Queensland State Secretary of the Federal Council for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Advancement in 1961 and campaigned successfully for amendments to the Constitution in 1967. Throughout her life, she advocated for cultural pride among First Nations people and also gained international acclaim for her writing, publishing 20 collections of poetry. Previously known as Kath Walker, she adopted the name Oodergeroo (paperbark tree) Noonuccal (her peoples, the traditional owners of Minjerribah) in 1988 to align with her identity as an Aboriginal woman and in protest against the Bicentennial celebrations.

audio.title: Kath Walker part 1
audio.transcript:
I would say that the majority of the Australian people voted Yes in favour of the Aboriginal people merely to clear their guilty conscience. Itâ€™s easy to put a mark on a ballot paper, and I must say this definitely, that there was a small minority group of sincere Australian people but I would say 75 [per cent] of those who voted Yes did it to clear their guilty conscience.

Incidentally, itâ€™s interesting to understand why those terrible discriminative laws were put into the books. In the first place, our civic fathers, or the white manâ€™s civic fathers of long ago, during the â€˜soothing of the dying pillowâ€™ era, the politicians, or the statesmen of that time, were writing over to Queen Victoria saying, â€˜The Aborigine is dying out.â€™ And true, he was â€“ they were poisoning him with strychnine in the waterholes and they were shooting him, and they were doing all sorts of things. And the Aborigine dropped from 300,000 strong to 80,000 in a very short period of time. So it was quite natural for them to say the Aborigine was a dying race.

Now it was during this period of time that the Constitution was being fixed, and as they thought we were a dying race, to save themselves a lot of bother they said, â€˜Well we will not count the Aborigines and we do not have to make laws for the Aborigines, because theyâ€™re going to die out anywayâ€™. And this is the reason today why Aboriginals have not had any education, any decent housing, any facilities that the white Australian enjoys today. Itâ€™s because of that stupid business of thinking the Aboriginals were going to die out.

Mind you, the Aboriginals are a determined lot, and theyâ€™re quite ungrateful. They didnâ€™t die, they lived on and are still living on; in spite of the many attempts to commit genocide and assassinate us all, we are still here. I think weâ€™ll last the white man out, truly.
audio.acknowledgements: This oral history of Kath Walker is from the De Berg Collection in the National Library of Australia. For more information, or to hear full versions of the recordings, visit the National Library of Australia website.

audio.title: Kath Walker part 2
audio.transcript:
In 1965 I think it was, we were invited to go in and talk to the then prime minister, Sir Robert Menzies. There was a deputation from all over Australia of Aboriginal spokesmen and women and we did go in. Sir Robert Menzies had told the public and the politicians, the people of the House, that he would not have a referendum in his lifetime as prime minister. Heâ€™d been badly beaten on the referendum before where he had appealed to the people to outlaw Communism and when the people said â€˜No outlawing of the Communist Partyâ€™, Sir Robert Menzies refused then to have anything to do with referendums in his lifetime as prime minister.

We lobbied the House of Parliament and itâ€™s to their discredit, really, that when we asked them to bring out the laws concerning the Aboriginal people that there was no laws, no books on the Aboriginal people in their archives or libraries, and they had to quickly have them printed, so that the politicians could read what it was, for and against the Aborigines. There was one, however, on the national â€“ the Canberra law book saying that if Aboriginals go into Canberra, any Justice of the Peace could declare them illegal immigrants into Canberra and they could be chased out of Canberra. This still applied to us, incidentally, at this period of time. And we always made a joke of it when we went to Canberra, you know, â€˜If you get into trouble, you know the law on the book. If a JP says Get Out, make sure you get your blanket,â€™ because the law still said that before sending them out of Canberra, they must first issue them with one government blanket. So we were determined weâ€™d get our government blanket if ever they threw us out.  
We told everyone this and we made it a laughingstock â€“ Canberra a laughingstock â€“ to such an extent that the first thing Sir Robert Menzies did was delete that off the Canberra constitution. So itâ€™s no longer there.
audio.acknowledgements: This oral history of Kath Walker is from the De Berg Collection in the National Library of Australia. For more information, or to hear full versions of the recordings, visit the National Library of Australia website.

audio.title: Ooodgeroo Noonuccal
audio.transcript:
This is a portrait of portrait of Quandamooka woman Oodgeroo Noonuccal, formerly known as Kath Walker, created by Clif Peir in 1965. Oodgerooo was an activist, poet, writer and educator.

The portrait is a framed oil painting on board, measuring 104 cm high and 83.7 cm wide with the frame having a depth of 5.1 cm.

Oodgeroo is a slim middle-aged woman, seated angled to the left against a dramatic and moody background. Behind her, dark greens merge into black. Highlights of emerald green flicker across the sky and a brighter lime green surrounds her head. Flecks of white suggest distant stars beyond this green-tinted atmosphere.  
Two sharp craggy hills in deep shadow appear in the lower third, to the left of the subject. In front of them a spindly leafless tree reaches its fine black branches into the sky. 

In the foreground, Oodgeroo sits in a straight-backed chair upholstered in soft turquoise cloth. Her face is framed by black curly hair cut just below her ears. Her skin is a deep rich brown. Soft light filters down from the upper left, creating a gentle sheen of lighter brown across her brow, cheeks, the tip of her nose and chin.

Her large dark eyes, framed by strong black brows, gaze out to her upper left. The play of light also emphasises her prominent cheek bones, straight nose and full closed lips.

Her neck is long and slim, with the muscles on either side of her jaw standing out, stretching down to her exposed clavicle.

Oodgeroo wears a simple round-necked white blouse underneath an elegant formal cerulean blue jacket with white edging on collar and sleeves, with a matching tailored straight skirt. The portrait ends just above her knees.  
Her hands lie on an open book in her lap, right hand over left. The pages, sepia flecked with white, are empty.

Her relaxed pose and distant gaze give a sense of thoughtful introspection.

Audio description written by Krysia Kitch and voiced by Amy Midddleby

Kondelea â€˜Dellaâ€™ Elliott (1917â€“2011) was a trailblazing union official and womenâ€™s rights lobbyist. In 1940 she was elected to the central council of the NSW branch of the Federated Clerksâ€™ Union. She became its assistant secretary in 1943, the first time a woman had held a senior role in the union. As a delegate to the NSW Labor Council and the ACTU, Elliott campaigned for equal pay for women. In the late 1940s and 50s she worked for the Waterside Workersâ€™ Federation, playing clandestine roles in the 1949 Australian coal strike and 1951 New Zealand wharf strike by supplying support funds then deemed illegal by authorities. Ivy Shore won the 1979 Portia Geach Memorial Award with this portrait, and used her prize money to have a studio built above the garage of her house in Sydneyâ€™s Woollahra. Shore gave the portrait to Elliott, who hung it in her home for many years.

Known as the â€˜Peopleâ€™s Generalâ€™, General Eva Burrows AC (1929â€“2015) was the first Australian woman world leader of the Salvation Army. Her parents were both Salvation Army officers, and she became an officer at age 22. During the 1950s and 60s Burrows worked as an educator in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) before becoming the principal of the Armyâ€™s International College for Officers in London in the 1970s. She later worked in Sri Lanka, Scotland and Naarm/Melbourne, contributing to causes including social services, youth unemployment and disaster relief. Elected as General in 1986, she championed women in leadership roles and oversaw the re-entry of the Salvation Army into Eastern Europe. \n\nGabrielle Martin painted Burrows with a statuette of Eva Booth, the first female General of the Salvation Army, and a sculpture that Burrows acquired in Zimbabwe.

****\n\nPurchased with funds provided by the Basil Bressler Bequest 2004 Aviator Nancy Bird Walton AO OBE (1915â€“2009) was known as the â€˜Angel of the Outbackâ€™ for her work flying medical professionals to remote communities. After receiving flying lessons with Charles Kingsford Smith, she obtained her pilotâ€™s licence in 1935 and was hired as the pilot for the Far West Childrenâ€™s Health Scheme that year. During the Second World War, Bird Walton was a commandant in the Womenâ€™s Air Training Corps and in 1950 she founded the Australian Women Pilotsâ€™ Association. Her 1990 autobiography _My God, Itâ€™s A Woman!_ took its title from one cattle station ownerâ€™s reaction to her emerging from the cockpit on a remote airstrip. In this portrait by Danelle Bergstrom, Bird Walton wears a wool suit in her favourite colour, pink. At her funeral in 2009 members of the Women Pilotsâ€™ Association dressed in this vibrant hue in honour of their late friend and pioneering mentor.

audio.title: Nancy Bird Walton part 1
audio.transcript:
If you want me to sum up my philosophy of life, well, what would I say? It matters not who you are but what you are. Doesnâ€™t matter what youâ€™ve got in your bank account, it matters what youâ€™ve got in your heart, and above all that, well, itâ€™s good to remember that above the clouds the sun is always shining.

Perhaps from those days, when I looked out from the verandah of our house at Collaroy out into the Pacific Ocean, saw that great expanse of Long Reef, the beach and the aeroplane that landed on it. You see, flying isnâ€™t very different. You take off, into the great open sky, you see the great beauty of the land that people climb mountains or rush up hills to see, and suddenly youâ€™re alone and completely and utterly responsible for yourself. And I think that thatâ€™s what makes flying people appreciate life so much and there is a sort of an artistic freedom in flying.

I think that flying people are different â€“ no better, no worse than other people â€“ but different. People whoâ€™ve flown solo, for itâ€™s the only thing in the world in which youâ€™re completely alone and completely and utterly responsible for yourself. You voluntarily remove yourself from your loved ones, from your way of life, from everything around you and you voluntarily return. You have to find that little scratch upon the face of the earth that is an airfield or something that you can land on, to come back and join the human race. So you have time to think, you have time to see things in their right setting, you have time to see how insignificant are the petty little jealousies, or ambitions and things of the world. And the scratches, literally the scratches, that man has made upon the surface of this great world, and perhaps you appreciate life more fully because of that, and try to look on the sunny side.
audio.acknowledgements: This oral history of Nancy Bird Walton is from the De Berg Collection in the National Library of Australia. For more information, or to hear full versions of the recordings, visit the National Library of Australia website.

audio.title: Nancy Bird Walton part 2
audio.transcript:
Iâ€™d first flown in 1930 and had made up my mind that I was going to learn to fly. And I had bought myself a helmet and goggles, because I had taken an instructional flight and nobodyâ€™s helmet was small enough for my head, so I had to have one made and then I studied books on aviation, away in the country, two hundred miles from any aeroplane. And when Kingsford Smith was coming to a town 13 miles away, on his barnstorming tour to the township of Wingham on the north coast of New South Wales, my sister and I decided that we would go in on the local cream truck and spend the day in Wingham and take a flight. Thatâ€™s when I first met him and talked to him and told him I was going to learn to fly. And he said, â€˜When you come to Sydney, come and see me, Iâ€™ll be starting my flying schoolâ€™, and nobody was more surprised than Kingsford Smith when I turned up on his doorstep and became his first pupil at his flying school at Mascot.

After I finished my training, I then decided the only way to stay in aviation was to get hold of an aeroplane, no matter how much of a rattletrap it was, and get out into the country and barnstorm. The idea was to fly over a town and circle it for several times and then people would come out to see the aeroplane or to go for a flight. And of course shows and race meetings, they just hopped across the fence or they just came over, and those who wanted to fly â€“ who were courageous enough to fly with these two young girls â€“ would pay ten shillings for a flight in our little Gypsy Moth, it was a Gypsy One Moth, open cockpit aeroplane.

There were always those people, especially the young people and children that wanted to fly. There were always those smart alecs who wanted to send their friend up but wouldnâ€™t go themselves, you know, and say, â€˜Give him the works, do some aerobatics, you know, loop the loop and do some spins and turn it inside outâ€™. And their great joy was to see their friend coming down looking green, but I donâ€™t think we involved ourselves much in this.
audio.acknowledgements: This oral history of Nancy Bird Walton is from the De Berg Collection in the National Library of Australia. For more information, or to hear full versions of the recordings, visit the National Library of Australia website.

The Hon Alex Chernov AC KC (b. 1938) is an Australian barrister, judge and the 28th Governor of Victoria. Throughout his career Chernov made significant contributions to legal education and leadership within the legal profession. Chernov served as Justice of the Supreme Court of Victoria and its Court of Appeal, chair of the Victorian Bar, president of the Law Council of Australia, and Chancellor of the University of Melbourne. Following his term as Governor of Victoria he was deputy to the Governor-General.\n\nThis work was a finalist in the National Portrait Galleryâ€™s 2020 _Darling Portrait Prize_. Artist Anne Middleton said of the work: â€˜His gaze is penetrating, measured and acutely observant. I have amplified his translucent skin using layers of opaque and transparent oil paint, conveying the complexity and subtlety of the man.â€™

Clifton Pugh AO is known for his portraits of political figures, including Labor politician and historian Clyde Cameron (1913â€“2008). Cameron worked as a shearer and union organiser before serving as a Member for Hindmarsh between 1949 and 1980, with 28 of these 31 years spent on the Opposition benches. In 1969, he allied himself with the ascending politician Gough Whitlam and was appointed Minister for Labour in 1972, and Minister for Labour and Immigration in 1974. Cameron became a prolific oral historian in the 1980s and 90s, recording a series of â€˜reminiscential conversationsâ€™ with people he had met through politics including Liberal figures such as Malcolm Fraser, Paul Hasluck, Nancy Buttfield and Garfield Barwick. This portrait of Cameron in a classic 1970s suit and tie features Pughâ€™s characteristic form, where limbs are elongated to expressive effect against a bold abstract background.

David Malet Armstrong AO (1926â€“2014) was an influential 20th-century Australian philosopher, whose research focused on the philosophy of mind and metaphysics. In the 1950s he lectured in philosophy at the University of London and the University of Melbourne, and in 1964 he became Challis Professor of Philosophy at the University of Sydney. He held this position, interrupted only by visiting professorships in the USA, until his retirement 28 years later. The best known of his 16 books, _A Materialist Theory of the Mind_ (1968), introduced the world to what has been termed â€˜Australian materialismâ€™, a theory that posits that mental states and brain processes are identical. In this painting, Clifton Pugh AO depicted his friend seated at a chessboard wearing the classic professor uniform: a brown suit.
