Atong Atem is a South Sudanese contemporary artist who lives and works in Naarm/Melbourne. In her portraits, many of which are self portraits, Atem pushes against the history of ethnographic photography by invoking the studio portraiture of mid-20th-century African photographers such as Malick SidibÃ© and Seydou KeÃ¯ta, for whom the camera provided a powerful means of resistance. Referencing these photographersâ€™ dynamic and vibrant compositions, as well as South Sudanese Dinka culture, Atem extends a lineage of photographic work that celebrates its subjects and returns agency to them. As she has said, â€˜Iâ€™m interested in the moment in history when black people took the camera and chose to photograph ourselves for ourselvesâ€™. In Atemâ€™s self portrait _Men In This Town 04_, the artist wears an acid green double-breasted suit and fedora, playfully using dress and pose to work through the complexities of gender and the performative codes of portraiture, while also paying homage to black dandyism and the importance of appearance and dressing up as documented by SidibÃ© and KeÃ¯ta.

video.title: Atong Atem
video.transcript:
My name is Atong Atem and I am a visual artist based in Melbourne. I work mostly with photography and video and tend to focus on portraiture.

The particular work that's here at the National Portrait Gallery, I'm wearing a lime green suit with a hat that's hiding my face a little bit and I'm sitting with a wide-legged stance, hands between my legs, staring quite sternly towards the camera. The series was really about me exploring presentation, especially when it comes to traditional photography on the African continent, that studio photography history, and how for so many people having the opportunity to be photographed was often a point of celebration or a significant moment, which meant that the way that people dressed and presented themselves to be photographed was quite formal, and if not formal, it was at least a moment to like truly express yourself and to present yourself in a way that is important. It was definitely intentional to make this particular work at that point in my life. And by that point I mean like post becoming a mother and having this new social identity and also in many ways having a new physical identity in the world and in the way that that body is interpreted, that body is sort of dictated.

I've done a lot of photographs that look at that feminine performance of properness or perfection or costume, and this was an opportunity to do a masculine investigation. So I was looking at my uncles, my siblings, my dad and other male figures, as well as men who are in parliament, in government, and looking at the way that they've reinterpreted colonial Western standards of proper presentation for men and masculinity.

Kaytetye artist, writer, director and cinematographer Warwick Thornton (b. 1970) was born and raised in Mparntwe/Alice Springs. _Samson and Delilah_ (2009), Thorntonâ€™s first feature film, won the CamÃ©ra dâ€™Or at the Cannes Film Festival and six Australian Film Institute awards including Best Director and Best Screenplay. His films _Sweet Country_ (2019) and _The New Boy_ (2023) also won numerous awards. As a cinematographer, Thorntonâ€™s credits include the documentaries _First Australians_ and _Art and Soul_, and the feature films _Radiance_ and _The Sapphires_.\n\nSusan Stitt ACS was the stills photographer and art director for _The Beach_, a six-part television series in which Thornton documented the months he spent living in a shack at Jilirr on the Dampier Peninsula in Western Australia. â€˜This photograph was taken inside a scene for the project,â€™ Stitt says, â€˜when he arrives at the beach, walks into Ancestral waters, weary and â€œcity screwed upâ€, and finds his balance.â€™ While Thornton removes his cowboy boots before plunging into the ocean, he retained his black suit and Akubra hat. Dunking his body in the water becomes a symbolic, and literal, act of cleansing.
Woollen coat pieces on wool and cotton backing\n\nCourtesy Vita Cochran and Anna Miles Gallery

Working predominantly with textiles, Sydney-based artist Vita Cochranâ€™s practice is deeply engaged with the histories of domestic craft and decoration. Cochranâ€™s _Quadraphonic Coats_ are assemblage works that combine repurposed fabric from assorted suit jackets. Cochran carefully picks apart each garment, literally deconstructing the symbolism of the suit and reimagining the pattern pieces into visually dynamic abstractions. The armholes are flattened out and stuck down as two-dimensional planes, and the back panels become separate forms. The air and volume that gives the suit its shape has all but evaporated. Occasional traces of wear remain apparent on the cloth as visceral reminders of the garmentsâ€™ previous lives, summoning the spectres of the people who wore them.

Yvonne Todd is renowned for highly stylised photographs that subtly distort our sense of reality. In _The Wall of Man_, a seemingly innocuous suite of corporate portraits, the sitters gaze confidently at us, formally dressed in suits and ties, but soon we realise that something doesnâ€™t quite fit. Bestowed with titles we expect to find on the doors of corner offices like â€˜Independent Manufacturing Directorâ€™ and â€˜Company Founderâ€™, the portraits come unstuck when we learn that the sitters were in fact selected by the artist following a callout for male models aged 65â€“75 in Toddâ€™s local newspaper. Each sitter was dressed by the artist in suits procured from local op shops. The ostensible banality of the images is further undercut by discrete details: the eerie glow of the Image Consultantâ€™s eyes, or the Senior Executiveâ€™s missing fingertip. Incrementally, the familiar becomes unfamiliar, such that these seemingly conventional representations of male authority and corporate power are undermined.

A multimedia artist best known for his video work, Grant Stevens combines text and moving image to satirical and sometimes destabilising effect. _Happiness_ features fragments of floating text gleaned from corporate training manuals, job applications and mindfulness meditations that slowly materialise on screen and intermix with increasing frequency, emulating the flurry of thoughts that often accompany anxiety spirals. Unshackled from the forms of figurative representation, this work can instead be read as a portrait of oneâ€™s internal dialogue intercut with corporate speak, revealing the complex oscillation between our professional and private personas.

Singer/songwriter Paul Kelly AO (b. 1955) made his performance debut in 1974 and has since released 30 studio albums and won many accolades, including 17 ARIA awards. Kaytetye writer, director and cinematographer Warwick Thornton was commissioned to create this portrait of Kelly for the musicianâ€™s biographical exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery in 2013. Conceiving this video, Thornton wrote: â€˜I want to get Paul to hold up a Marshall amp â€“ its weight bearing down on him â€“ as he gently spins in a clockwise direction on a revolving platform. Paul will be dressed in his favourite suit and we will rig an amp to rest gently on his shoulders in a moodily lit studio. The idea is that the amp represents a heavy burden, music is a heavy burden, but Paulâ€™s strength as a singer/songwriter is shown through him being a strong pillar â€“ able to bear the weight of this heavy responsibility.â€™
pigment photographic print

â€˜This portrait was taken in Davidâ€™s basement, putting his last load of washing through before going off to Perth for some time and then onto London indefinitely. He had decided to give acting his all. Davidâ€™s portrait is part of my larger ongoing project, _CITIZEN_, spanning 30 years and 60+ countries, using the same strict parameters while taking portraits in arbitrary moments and often random encounters.â€™\n\nSwedish-born photographer Ingvar Kenne is based on Gadigal Land in Sydney. His portraits, all of which adhere to the square composition of medium-format film, carry an immediacy and candidness that enables the individuality of each subject to emerge.

â€˜This photo collage layers a childhood photograph of my cousin Rashida over a page from _EBONY_ magazine, bringing my family archive into dialogue with formative cultural experiences from the 1980s. It situates this private history alongside a publication of liberation, long described as â€œby us, for usâ€. Produced by the Johnson Publishing Company from 1945 to 2016, _EBONY_ chronicled Black life in the US across social justice, health, beauty, fashion, sport and education. Through this act of overlay and assemblage, familial memory engages with broader histories â€“ aligning Rashidaâ€™s image with _EBONYâ€™s_ visual language to bridge temporal distance and expand my understanding of Blackness today.â€™\n\nArini Byng is a multidisciplinary artist born on Gadigal Country and now based in Naarm/Melbourne. She explores how moments, objects and places appear within social and political debates and activates her family archive to navigate themes of identity, history and lived experience.
pigment photographic print

â€˜My aunty migrated to Australia from Thailand when I was born. When this portrait was taken she was the last surviving member of her generation in my immediate family, an important figure who helped forge and sustain a relationship with our cultural legacy. This image was captured the evening she experienced a debilitating fall, one of many similar medical scares in the preceding months which relayed how delicate this portal to my heritage is. Insisting she bathe herself independently after this incident, her resilience in this vulnerable state captures the strength and intimacy of the bonds which have shaped my sense of cultural pride and belonging.â€™\n\nNathan Beard is a multidisciplinary artist based in Naarm/Melbourne. His work draws from his Australian-Thai heritage and explores family history, archives and broad signifiers of â€˜Thainessâ€™ to expose the porous influences which shape the commercial and historical production of culture.
