â€˜Set in France, _Sisterhood_ responds to the countryâ€™s 2022 hijab ban in basketball and the wider exclusion of visibly Muslim women from sport. Against a backdrop of rising Islamophobia and far-right politics, _Sisterhood_ documents the resilience of those affected and the activism of collectives like Basket pour Toutes (Basketball for all). This portrait challenges policies that silence and marginalise under the guise of secularism, affirming that the right to play â€“ and to choose how to exist â€“ is fundamental to gender justice.â€™\n\nSu Cassiano is a French-Italian photographer who settled in Australia in 2016. Currently based in Istanbul, TÃ¼rkiye, she specialises in narrative portraiture and documentary. Grounded in collaboration and trust, Cassiano fosters meaningful relationships with her subjects, resulting in portraits that are imbued with emotional nuance and authenticity.
diptych: pigment photographic prints

â€˜This is a portrait of my father, LÃª Ngá»c Long, who had served in the Vietnam military since he was 14. As 2025 marked the 50th anniversary of the end of the American War in Vietnam, I asked my father to commemorate the occasion as if he was being directed by his unit lieutenant. The photographs were made through an infrared filter â€“ a technology used by America during its war in Vietnam. In doing so, I aim to subvert the filterâ€™s original role in exposing Vietnamese figures during combat and instead gesture toward the complex emotions within my fatherâ€™s wartime experience.â€™\n\nPhuong Nguyen Le is a Vietnamese photographer, artist and researcher based in Naarm/Melbourne. His work engages with counter-historical narratives and draws on familial, communal and collective identities within his communities.
pigment photographic print

â€˜_His Nibs_ is a collaboration between my mother Dorothy Jean Croft (nÃ©e Stone, 1938â€“2010), my father Joseph Croft (c. 1925â€“1996) and myself as the artist and their eldest child. My handsome father stands proudly in front of his two-tone EK Holden at Mt Isa Airport, where he had been working as a surveyor on the Townsville to Mt Isa railway line. The portrait was taken by my mother shortly after her arrival from â€œdown southâ€ as a marker of their reuniting after a lengthy period apart. The title _His Nibs_ is an affectionate, cheeky nod in my motherâ€™s hand to my fatherâ€™s confident stance in the image.â€™\n\nBrenda L Croft is from the Gurindji/Malngin/Mudburra Peoples, Victoria River region of the Northern Territory, and has Anglo-Australian/Chinese/German/Irish/Scottish heritage. For four decades Croft has played a leading role in the cultural arts sector as a multidisciplinary creative-led researcher and artist.
pigment photographic print

â€˜This work is a portrait of my friend Aitor and is part of an ongoing series on connection within the queer community. I am an Australian photographer, Aitor is a Spanish painter, and we made this photograph in his bedroom in London. The image itself offers no explicit markers of place. Instead, we have an intimate shared moment shaped by transience, trust and the quiet negotiations of being elsewhere. I enjoy the ambiguity of the portraits in this series. Is this a moment of rest, after intimacy, or a quiet staging of solitude? Thatâ€™s up to you.â€™\n\nLos Angeles-based Australian photographer Luke Austin is known for his tender portraits of members of the gay, queer and trans community that reveal the sitterâ€™s individuality in a moment of disarming connection.
pigment photographic print

â€˜This image features Eva in her home in Canberra and was shot as part of a series of portraits titled _Make this house a home_. All of the portraits begin with a conversation about how each subject feels connected to their bodies. We work through gestures, searching for easing of tension, searching for vigour. How do you make a home from this shell youâ€™ve been given? Like spaces, our bodies hold history, memory and evidence of our experiences; the site for our hopes, dreams, anxieties and fears to play out.â€™\n\nMadeline Bishop is a Naarm/Melbourne-based photographer whose work focuses on the dynamics of relationships and how people interact socially. Bishop creates scenes that are staged yet candid, interrogating the tension between the real and the performative.
pigment photographic print

â€˜This portrait depicts Eedo/Aunt Khadija, a resident of the Flemington public housing estate and a community organiser opposing its demolition. She asked that the image convey the suddenness with which her life in a close-knit community is being upended through evictions amid a state-wide redefinition of public housing. The photograph forms part of _What Remains?_, an ongoing project looking at how communities in Melbourne sustain social life in areas undergoing rapid change. It explores themes of perseverance in the face of broad social and economic disruptions that quietly, yet continually, stir earlier experiences of displacement.â€™\n\nHussein Abdirahman Mohamud is a photographer based in Naarm/Melbourne. His practice examines how lived environments are shaped by memory.
type C photograph

â€˜This is a portrait of Ava. In Avaâ€™s words: â€œI could go forever and ever. Arousal enters from below and owing to gravity it struggles to exit. An upward stretch is a desire path â€“ I wander off road only uphill, only listening to Dido.â€â€™\n\nCamille Perry is a queer Naarm/Melbourne-based artist whose research-based practice engages with queer archives and the passage of time. Through photographic and film production Perry considers how technologies designed to preserve memory sometimes expose its fragility.
pigment photographic print

â€˜Creating staged portraits of fictional characters lights my fire. Even more so, finding collaborators who immediately understand the absurdity and jump on board brings me pure joy. Actor Maria Angelico and I exchanged some texts about dog shows then BAM, within hours we had wigs, costumes, her dog Peta and a two-hour community hall booking. The result is â€œLeithâ€, who is trying to earn respect from a community who donâ€™t like him. Heâ€™s entered the dog show for acknowledgment, but Peta doesnâ€™t respect him either. She performs for cameras, but the second after this shot, she bolts. Leith plods after, humiliated.â€™ \n\nPhotographer Jo Duck lives and works in Naarm/Melbourne. Driven by an appreciation for all things camp, joyful and absurd, Duckâ€™s photography centres on crafting unique characters who live confidently in worlds of their own.
pigment photographic print

â€˜In this series, I use archival Dior hats to investigate the tension between mid-century decorum and contemporary excess. As an immigrant, I encountered the â€œtrashyâ€ imagery of the Melbourne Cup long before moving to Australia. These scenes of public euphoric intoxication, often swept under the rug, became a significant contemporary cultural reference point for me. By restaging an iconic Cup photo in drag, I pair the elegance of a 1960s Dior hat with the debris on the grass. This performance transforms a high-status artefact into a tool for queer spectacle, interrogating the shifting associations of class, fashion and national identity.â€™\n\nHong Kong-born Scotty So is a Naarm/Melbourne-based artist. Driven by the thrill of camp, he explores the often-contradictory relationship between humour and sincerity, creating fictional scenes that slightly distort our sense of the familiar.
pigment photographic print

â€˜This portrait depicts Kai in an abandoned brickworks quarry in Lismore, New South Wales. In a region where infrastructure remains limited after floods, the quarry offers teenagers a place to gather beyond authority. Wrapped in a towel, Kai brushes her long, wet hair, a tender act usually reserved for a private space. Set within a public swimming site, the portrait reminds us that experiences of intimacy, care and coming of age often unfold in improvised landscapes. The image is from the ongoing series _The Quarry_, which traces the ways young people carve out spaces of freedom and belonging.â€™\n\nTajette Oâ€™Halloran is a photographic artist from Bundjalong Country in Lismore. Her work investigates the social and emotional terrain of adolescence, identity and belonging within the context of regional Australia.
pigment photographic print

â€˜This photograph depicts my wife and I, on the cusp of welcoming another child into our family. 12 years of friendship has seen us through a lot. There have been good times and there have been bad times; chronic health issues, the grief of her being disowned by her family, a traumatic birth and unravelling from the postpartum anxiety/depression that followed. At times the whole world feels like itâ€™s broken and burning down around us, yet still we push on with quiet optimism. Where thereâ€™s love, thereâ€™s space to dream. One where a brighter future is more than just a glimmer of hope.â€™\n\nShea Kirk is a Naarm/Melbourne-based artist who works with traditional photographic methods and techniques. Paring back photography to its fundamentals, Kirk works with both commercially available and self-made cameras, honouring the essential components of photography â€“ as a recording of light â€“ in an intentional and thoughtful way.
diptych: pigment photographic prints

â€˜This portrait of Ettael is a double exposure diptych taken while researching family trees, queerness, toxicity and healing. Each photograph was exposed across two sites: the decommissioned Nufarm Factory in Fawkner, Victoria, along the banks of the Merri Creek, and the AIDS Memorial Garden outside the old Infectious Diseases Hospital in Fairfield. These sites of toxicity, death, contamination, grief, and now regeneration, are places we feel compelled to photograph, care and make from. The double exposure resists imagined enclosure, countering the idea that supposedly containable units of oneâ€™s family, body, identity and history are sealed in some way.â€™\n\nArtists Abbra Kotlarczyk and Briony Galligan live and work on Wurundjeri and Boonwurrung Country in Naarm/Melbourne. They collaborate to create works that explore the realities of labour, care and ecology within the queer experience.

labels.title: Kanjdjihkanjdji Madjinbardi Kukabo (Down by the River at Madjinbardi)
labels.subtitle: Shannon Nango

text.content: digital print

â€˜This is my favourite place. I grew up beside this river. My family and I always came down here for fishing, swimming and dry season camping. When I come here, I think about happy childhood times when I used to camp here with my mum, my dad and my grandparents. Sadly, crocodiles live here now so we canâ€™t swim or camp here anymore.â€™\n\nMirarr photographer Shannon Nango is a Kunwinjku language speaker and a djungkayin (caretaker) for the Madjinbardi area, near Jabiru in Kakadu National Park in the Northern Territory. Nangoâ€™s photographs document his connection to Kunred (his homeland).

labels.title: Three Siblings: Chromatograms of Emmie, Rasmus and Cosmos
labels.subtitle: Sammy Hawker

text.content: pigment photographic print

â€˜Three chromatograms of three beloved children â€“ Emmie, Rasmus and Cosmos â€“ described by their mother as her sun, her moon and her stars. Chromatography is a camera-less photographic process used to facilitate the visual expression of natural materials. The hues and patterns that form over the silver nitrate-soaked paper cannot be predetermined or controlled. Chromatograms can be thought of as self portraits of the materials used to create them. These chromatograms were created using Emmieâ€™s hair, Rasmusâ€™ placenta and the tissue of Cosmosâ€™ body â€“ Cosmos miscarried at 15 weeks and lives among the stars. Siblings of aether and earth.â€™\n\nSammy Hawker is a visual artist who works predominantly on Ngunnawal/Ngambri Country in the Canberra region. She uses experimental photographic techniques to co-create imagery with environmental elements. Her work reflects on how knowledge and memory is inscribed in materials, places and bodies.

labels.title: Coming Home
labels.subtitle: Prue Hazelgrove
labels.medium: tintype scan, archival pigment print on cotton

text.content: tintype scan, archival pigment print on cotton

â€˜The week before Morgs had top surgery, we camped by this pool in Tallaganda, New South Wales. They stood bare beneath the full moon, the stars and gums, in this place that has held us both through many trials and triumphs, farewelling a form that never quite fit them. Returning to the same pool, the water now reflects a body that feels like home. â€œThe breeze kisses my scars, both physical and within. For the forest is no stranger to the strange. I breathe and I belong.â€â€™\n\nLiving on Ngunnawal/Ngambri Country in Canberra, Prue Hazelgrove is a queer artist who specialises in the 19th-century wet plate collodion process. Their use of this early photographic technique, with its deep connection to history and tradition, enables them to represent stories that have been historically erased from the narrative.
pigment photographic print

â€˜Tina and her teenage son lived in their car on and off for almost two years before they sought refuge in North Lismore, joining others occupying flood-affected homes amid the ongoing housing crisis in regional Australia. The damaged house they have been living in is due to be demolished as part of a government scheme to move people out of high-risk flood zones, yet Tina says there is little affordable accommodation available for women escaping violence. â€œWe have water, a toilet, a shower,â€ she says. For Tina, the room offers rare stability, a place to rest after years spent in survival mode.â€™\n\nElise Derwin is a documentary photographer based on Bundjalung Country in Lismore, New South Wales. Her work focuses on regional communities shaped by crisis, environmental risk and long-term change.
inkjet photographic print

â€˜My relationship with my wife Margaux has felt akin to the story of Hades and Persephone. We met in Paris but have since lived in Australia. Like Hades who brought Persephone to the underworld, I brought Margaux â€œdown underâ€, away from her family and friends in France. Navigating this cross-cultural relationship has had its challenges. As a child born to Chinese immigrants, I understand the pain and the beauty of creating a home far from home. Using papercuts and light, I embrace a world of shadows.â€™\n\nMeng-Yu Yan é¢œæ¢¦é’° is a Chinese-Australian queer non-binary artist based on Wallumedegal Land in Sydney. Their practice explores ideas of self-reflection, absence and alienation.
pigment photographic print

â€˜This photograph shows my daughter sitting quietly on her own. I was nearby, watching from a short distance. She didnâ€™t look back, and she didnâ€™t need to. I felt the urge to step closer and chose not to. The moment was brief, but it stayed with me. Being close didnâ€™t mean stepping forward. Loving her meant learning when to stay still.â€™\n\nFranky Tsang is a photographer who works on Gamaragal/Cammeraygal Country in Sydney. His portraiture practice is grounded in emotional sensitivity and human connection, and focuses on subtle, often unspoken moments.
type C photograph

â€˜I photographed Australian author Bri Lee in my studio, creating a portrait that feels quiet and painterly. Known for her incisive prose and public voice, I sought her inward gaze â€“ a contemplative presence that mirrors the interior world of her work: thoughtful, composed and quietly resolute.â€™\n\nSaskia Wilson is a photographer who lives and works on Gadigal and Bidjigal Land in Sydney. She uses digital and analogue photographic techniques to explore the ephemerality and emotional dimension of image making.
type C photograph

â€˜This photograph was taken during the making of a video work. Puppeteer Nguyen CÃ´ng ChÃ­nh performs with ChÃº Tá»…u, a character in the world of water puppetry who guides the audience through the narrative and plot points of a water play. In the video, ChÃº Tá»…u goes for a swim and performs an unspoken soliloquy to a landscape that he has developed a deep longing for, but can never belong to. The water here is something he recognises, yet it tastes different. His customary practices become unfamiliar here. The water feels and sounds like a different place. ChÃº Tá»…u is no longer a guide. He is a temporary visitor, an uninvited guest.â€™\n\nVietnam-born James Nguyen lives and works in Naarm/Melbourne. His interdisciplinary practice traverses cinematography, photography, text and performance, and engages with decolonial thinking and the expression of what he has termed the â€˜diasporic absurdâ€™.

labels.title: Uncle Mervyn Bishop - Australiaâ€™s first Aboriginal press photographer
labels.subtitle: Dean Saffron

text.content: gelatin silver photograph

â€˜Uncle Mervyn Bishop, a proud Kamilaroi man and Australiaâ€™s first Aboriginal press photographer, reflects quietly just before his 80th birthday. His lifeâ€™s work has helped shape the visual history of this nation, documenting moments of truth, dignity and change. For decades, his photographs created a record that ensured Aboriginal people were seen with honesty and authority. In this portrait, I wanted to honour Uncle Mervâ€™s presence at this milestone, acknowledging the weight of what he has witnessed and preserved. His legacy continues to influence how stories are told and remembered across Australia.â€™\n\nDean Saffron is a proud Kamilaroi/Gomeroi photographer and filmmaker based on Kabi Kabi and Jinibara Country on the Sunshine Coast, Queensland. His practice centres on respectful, collaborative portraiture and long-form storytelling with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
pigment photographic print

â€˜Although Star, my little sister, may need a carer for the rest of her life, she is one of the most caring people I know. She carries her own set of challenges that come from living with Autism and an intellectual disability, as well as responsibilities that come with being part of a big family. Having recently graduated Year 12, Star is stepping into a year of change in 2026. What I wanted to capture is the side of her that we see and love every day â€“ her strength, tenderness and care. Here, she comforts our nephew who just woke up from sleep.â€™\n\nTace Stevens is a Noongar/Spinifex visual storyteller based in Boorloo/Perth, Western Australia. She uses photography and film to explore the world around her, and to better understand who she is as an Aboriginal woman.
pigment photographic print

****

â€˜In the past, â€œwalkaboutâ€ meant journeying on foot, expanding knowledge for future generations. In this image, my long-term friend/model/muse Joey Gala crosses Tokyoâ€™s Shibuya Crossing, wearing Gucci head to toe (albeit barefoot: connected to Country). Since I began making art in 2010, Joeyâ€™s persona and image have been integral to my work. This photographic portrait places Joey at the heart of Japanâ€™s commercial district, memorialising aspects of Japanese culture, and continues my exploration of the contradictions and eccentricities of identity. We identify and are conditioned by experience. Joeyâ€™s will also inform those to come, creating a stronger future.â€™ 

Michael Cook is a Meanjin/Brisbane-based contemporary photographic artist of Bidjara heritage. Over the last decade, Cook has produced works that interrogate the legacy of colonisation and invite the viewer to experience roles in reversal and histories re-written.
lambda photographic print

â€˜Mum. This identity is not something I wear temporarily â€“ it is a state of constant collaboration. My children and I live in ongoing exchange; they shape me as much as I shape them. We share routines, mundane ritual, atoms. The idea of mutual imprinting, of porous boundaries between self and other, is at the heart of my work. This multi-stage collaborative work began with a candid portrait taken in my kitchen. A print was made and I Blu-Tacked it to the wall. I invited my kids to hand-colour it as they wished. They left and revisited and revisited it again.â€™\n\nMia Mala McDonald is a Naarm/Melbourne-based photographer with a socially engaged practice who often works with portraiture. Her work focuses on people, identity and family, with an emphasis on LGBTQIA+ representation in Australia.
type C photograph

â€˜_Blak & Bare_ is a reclamation for First Nations people. It depicts the strength, resilience and sovereignty of every single one of us. Venita Mooney (the model) is a Yuwi, Meriam Mir and South Sea Islander woman. Her natural essence is one of softness, fierceness and inspiration. She is connected to her culture and is an artist at heart. Surrounded by the sea, bare, she shows that no matter what way the tide pulls, against or for us, we are still here. Our culture will never die. We still live on and continue to tell our stories.â€™\n\nTiarni Majid-Loban is a proud Wuthathi woman with connections to the Torres Strait who lives and works on Yuwi Country/Mackay, Queensland. In her photography practice she focuses on family and connection to place, documenting the present for the future.
pigment photographic print

â€˜_The Falling_ was photographed in Croajingolong National Park, Victoria, on Gunaikurnai and Bidawal Country. The figure in the image, Gretel Taylor, is a dance artist, curator and researcher known for her site-specific performance work that uses movement to interrogate colonial relationships to land. This collaborative work was made as a response to the excess, greed and inertia of those with the power to enact change at this moment of ecological collapse. She hopes we can catch ourselves on the way down.â€™ \n\nLaki Sideris is a Naarm/Melbourne-based photographer and filmmaker who regularly collaborates with Gretel Taylor. Taylorâ€™s performance practice presents dance as a mode of sensing and moving with the surrounding environment.
pigment photographic print

â€˜Jason, my close friend, was photographed at dayâ€™s edge, the sun behind him casting his figure into silhouette. In his hand is a small keepsake, a reminder of Jordan, his daughter, who died by suicide. Jason is creating a documentary about his experience, telling his story in his own words, and pushing back against the silence that often surrounds suicide and grief. I made this portrait in open country to hold space for that work, and the weight of what cannot be undone.â€™\n\nAdam Edwards lives and works on Wilyakali Country in Broken Hill, New South Wales. He takes inspiration from the stories of people in regional Australia as well as the rugged beauty and charm of the outback.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2020 Finalist

â€˜I work as an artist, academic and virtual reality filmmaker, connecting my own experiences to wider social, cultural and political contexts. As a Bidjara person of the central Queensland desert, I have often drawn a vivid connection to the environment throughout my 20-year practice. This self portrait references the collective anxiety and uncertainty of the climate threat that defines our times. The title is a well-known colloquialism for a situation both impending and unavoidable. Cascading wattle blossoms act as a ticking clock. Using my signature native botanical elements, I disappear into the constellation of flowers â€“ beautiful, regenerative and ephemeral.â€™\n\nDr Christian Thompson AO is a Bidjara/Irish/Chinese-Australian contemporary artist based in Naarm/Melbourne. His declarative self portraiture often features native flowers that symbolically reflect ideas of identity, kinship, culture and connection to Country.

labels.title: Where have all the flowers gone
labels.subtitle: The Huxleys, Garrett Huxley and Will Huxley

text.content: pigment photographic print on paper\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2022 Finalist

â€˜_Where have all the flowers gone_ explores the florid magic of the natural world, embracing the soft romance of flowers and their sexual allure. The image embraces all the things we were denied as boys growing up in homophobic and traditionally masculine suburban environments. It captures the surreal sparkling beauty of two queer lovers refusing to descend into the darkness, as bold and bright as a flower, imbued with the essence of Jean Genetâ€™s autobiographical novel _Our Lady of the Flowers_ (1943).â€™\n\nWill Huxley and Garrett Huxley are Naarm/Melbourne-based collaborative visual and performance artists. The Huxleysâ€™ works traverse the categories of costume, film and photography in what they describe as a visual assault of sparkle, surrealism and the absurd.
pigment photographic print on paper\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2023 Finalist

â€˜When this portrait was taken Shirley was 92. One of 14 children, and unable to read or write, she spent her working life cleaning schools and private homes, eventually paying off her own house through her earnings. She describes herself as a â€œno-frills womanâ€ and is comfortable in the body she inhabits. Her self-assurance reflects a life of hard work, resilience and independence. This portrait is part of _No Filter: Women at Home in Their Skin_, an intimate series of women over 70, photographed in their own homes with little concealed. The work responds to the near invisibility of the ageing female body, foregrounding visibility, representation and agency.â€™\n\nFrancis Cloake is a photographer based on the lands of the Bundjalung Nation in Cavanbah/Northern Rivers, New South Wales. Cloakeâ€™s portraiture practice centres on people, place and the stories that connect them.

labels.title: The Honourable Bob Hawke Savouring a Strawberry Milkshake
labels.subtitle: Harold David

text.content: pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2018 People's Choice Award

â€˜All the planning in the world went out the window the moment Bob Hawke walked into the room, sipping through a pink straw. As my father used to say, â€œWhat it is!â€, and at that moment, as history stood before me, I understood what he meant! I am always looking for what connects us all and makes us human. My heart knows we are created equal, and I always strive to capture that essence in my photographs â€“ a takeaway cup, a glint in the eyes, a life well-lived.â€™\n\nHarold David is a multidisciplinary artist based on Darug and Gundungurra Land in the Blue Mountains, New South Wales. Formerly a fashion and portrait photographer known for his playful, irreverent works, David is now focused on his abstract painting practice.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2021 Finalist

â€˜The fires that swept across Victoria in the summer of 2019â€“20 drove thousands to the edge of the sea, where encircling flames and amber-red skies left no path to safety but by water. This photograph captures 11-year-old Finn, steady and resolute, bravely fleeing Mallacoota by boat, with his younger brother, mum and family dog on board.â€™\n\nAllison Marion lives on the lands of the Bidwell (Bidawal), Gunaikurnai and Monero (Ngarigo) peoples in East Gippsland, Victoria. Her photography practice is inspired by the landscapes and seascapes of the region, and often focuses on fleeting light and candid moments.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2020 Winner

â€˜Josh Niland, head chef and owner of Saint Peter restaurant, is reinventing what can be done with fish, and â€“ most importantly â€“ with every part of the fish, in a huge effort to drastically reduce wastage. His trailblazing work has received enormous praise from the likes of Jamie Oliver and Nigella Lawson.â€™\n\nRob Palmer is a photographer based on Gadigal Land/Sydney who works across the genres of portraiture, food and lifestyle. Collaborating with many of Australiaâ€™s most influential chefs and food identities, his work focuses on creating honest portraits that celebrate the people behind the stories.

labels.title: Dwayne John, off-siding a commercial kangaroo shooter, Adnyamathanha Country, Plumbago Station, South Australia
labels.subtitle: Adam Ferguson

text.content: pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2018 Finalist

â€˜Dwayne John, from Broken Hill, works as a kangaroo shooterâ€™s offsider. 70 times a night, after a roo jolts and falls in the spotlight, Dwayne hauls the carcass onto the back of a truck. I made this picture of Dwayne in the early hours of a hot morning on Plumbago Station in South Australia. To me, Dwayne holding this kangaroo symbolises the human attempt to tame the land. This work is from my series _Big Sky_, which aims to challenge and position archetypal tropes of Australian identity within the complex realities of contemporary life in the countryâ€™s arid interior.â€™ \n\nAdam Ferguson lives and works on Wurundjeri Country in Naarm/Melbourne. Within his broader practice, Ferguson has photographed international conflicts while also examining the impacts of globalisation and climate change on regional Australia.
pigment photographic print on paper\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2024 Finalist

â€˜Micky is my cousin. It was the middle of the wet season and in between fishing places, we were all relaxing when this beetle dropped onto his face. He was a little shocked, but he gathered himself, pulled the clinging beetle off his face and let it wander off to live yet another day. I love spending time on the river with my family. The river is filled with invertebrates; they are the backbone of biodiversity, and they call the Coen River home too. Itâ€™s a shared space. I wanted to capture this connection and show that we can all live in harmony with nature and its diversity of species. Life is fragile.â€™\n\nSouthern Kaantju/Umpila artist Naomi Hobson lives on the banks of the Coen River in Coen, Queensland. Her paintings, ceramics and photographs address the powerful and ancient links between Country and identity.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2015 Winner

â€˜Soobatan Village, in northern Iran. It sits in a mountain range so high, it exists above the clouds. They call it â€œthe dream of Iranâ€. In this village, I was told, the cleverest kids are sent to city-schools to be taught; the rest are made to stay, and most become shepherds. Ali was one of them. It was a warm morning. As I was walking, I saw him approaching through the mist that permanently clings to the road. Ali looked at me and my camera enquiringly. He said very little â€“ mostly one word, over and over: _alooche_. It means â€œlittle berryâ€.â€™\n\nHoda Afshar is a Naarm/Melbourne-based visual artist who works with photography and the moving image. Her practice focuses on the intricate relationships between photography and power and uses the camera to both probe, and subvert, the relationship between visibility and violence.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2018 Finalist

â€˜This portrait of champion Australian ballroom dancer Lyu Masuda is from my ongoing series of analogue, black-and-white, double-exposure photographs made with a 35mm film camera. The process allows me to combine one exposure with another in ways that cannot be fully anticipated. I am interested in the misalignments, chance compositions and unexpected relationships that emerge through this technique. Having worked with portraiture for many years, this series brings together images of flowers with individuals from LGBTQIA+ communities.â€™\n\nDavid Rosetzky is a Naarm/Melbourne-based artist who works across photography, video, installation and performance. Often working in collaboration with his sitters, Rosetzky creates layered photographs with multiple exposures, echoing the fluidity of identity and queer experience.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2019 Finalist

â€˜I made this photograph during a visit to my home country, Belgium, in the summer of 2018. On a nightly walk through the countryside, my wife, Celia Hindmarsh, discovered this watchtower and climbed up to look out over the cornfields.â€™\n\nWouter Van de Voorde is a Belgian-born photographer based on Ngunnawal/Ngambri Country in Canberra. Using analogue processes, his work focuses on the quirks and nuances of Australian culture.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2021 Finalist

â€˜One thing that this last year [2020] has reminded me is that I donâ€™t have to travel far to find beauty in my environment and the inspiration to create photographs. It is there in my home, when I walk out on our property, and within the people and places I am surrounded by. As a return to my early _Friends_ series, I spent time focusing on the people close to me: my family, my friends and their children. This photograph depicts the three Goodall brothers living beautifully close to the land, running barefoot, playing in the cornfields surrounding their property.â€™\n\nBased on Dharawal Land near Berry, New South Wales, Tamara Deanâ€™s multidisciplinary practice spans photography, installation, moving image and public art. Her work explores the evolving relationship between humans and the natural world, addressing themes of ecological fragility and vulnerability.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2007 Finalist

â€˜For two years I documented my family, friends and relatives for my series _The Christmas Tree Bucket_ that looks at Christmas and special occasions. The photographs focus on the private moments and quiet exchanges of family members as they take time out from the hurly burly normally associated with such celebrations. This portrait is of my son Jem, lost in his own world at the end of the day during the Christmas period.â€™\n\nTrent Parke lives and works in Tarntanya/Adelaide and is the first Australian to become a Full Member of the Magnum Photo Agency. His work offers an emotional and psychological portrait of family life that is poetic and often darkly humorous.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2017 Finalist

â€˜This image is part of an ongoing series of photographs of refugees and immigrants in Melbourne. Fatima is from Pakistan and had recently settled here with her two young children, while her husband remained in Pakistan to finish his studies. I chose Fatima as a subject because her resilience in the face of adversity found her a home, in Australia, where she finally belongs. Fatima said: â€œI wanted to leave them respectfully, I wanted to leave them forever. And I did that. Iâ€™m quite successful â€¦ Things are better here for me. There is truly nothing I miss from Pakistan.â€â€™\n\nAnu Kumar is a photographic artist based in Naarm/Melbourne. Working primarily with medium-format photography, she photographs gentle everyday experiences that resonate with broader themes of displacement, memory and the reconstruction of home across borders.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2007 Finalist

â€˜I took this portrait of Rosemary as part of a series of portraits of teenage girls I was working on in 2006. Rosemary was 17 years old and working full-time as a carer in an aged nursing home.â€™\n\nPetrina Hicks lives and works on Gadigal Land/ Sydney. Working primarily with staged, studio photography, Hicks creates meticulously composed portraits that explore depictions of women and feminine symbolism drawn from art history and mythology.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2019 Finalist

â€˜This is a portrait of South African-born Australian singer Troye Sivan. Perth-raised, Sivan gained popularity as a young teen singing on YouTube and in Australian talent competitions, before signing with a major label in 2013. In the same year, at the age of 18, Sivan made a YouTube video announcing that he was gay, determined to not pursue a career in entertainment while staying in the closet. He was part of a growing group of high-profile younger singers who insist on being open about their sexuality as they make their way in the industry.â€™\n\nBased on Gadigal Land/Sydney James Brickwood is a staff photographer at _The Sydney Morning Herald_ and a member of the Australian collective Oculi. His work often captures underground and youth subcultures and their relationship to music.
pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2011 Finalist

â€˜In this series, I asked many of the fashion models I worked with to be photographed immediately on arrival at the studio before they subject themselves to hair and makeup. They still have the energy and vibrancy of the street about them, counterbalanced by the stillness that is demanded by the technique of shooting with available light with low depth of field. My intent with this series was to collaboratively create an intensity and engagement, an exchange of power and energy. Pulling up this file from my archive 16+ years later I looked into Samanthaâ€™s eyes, and myself reflected in them, and was transported to a different version of me, inhabiting a vastly changed world.â€™\n\nHamish Ta-mÃ© lives and works on Tharawal Land in the Southern Highlands, New South Wales. Alongside his commercial practice, he creates street-style portraits that examine the tension between stillness and motion, and isolation and connection.
pigment photographic print on paper\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2024 Art Handlersâ€™ Award

â€˜After three years apart, three precious weeks reunited me with Mum. I felt Iâ€™d never truly seen her as herself; her anxieties, fears, regrets and affections had been shielded from view so that she could become this mother of mine. Yet, for the first time, tear-stained, she told me stories I had never known. She exuded childlike joy among orchids and succulents. Her hand sought mine on our walks. Youâ€™ve loved as much as you can, Chunyi. And Iâ€™ve started to see that now, Mother.â€™\n\nShelley Xue is a Naarm/Melbourne-based artist and arts worker from Guangdong, China. Her practice engages photography, personal objects and archives as ways of remembering, reconnecting and reflecting on family and home.

labels.title: She Fell Asleep During the Movie
labels.subtitle: Grant Hawkes

text.content: pigment photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2007 Finalist

â€˜The sitter in my portrait is Tomiko Tateno. She fell asleep during a documentary we were watching on Robert Capa. Our tea, cigarettes and other things are scattered about the floor. This image explores the significance of objects and their assumed symbolism in portraiture. At the time I was interested in using photographic reportage to capture quiet moments rather than the significant occasions which would normally define that kind of photography. Looking back on this photograph after 20 years, Iâ€™m drawn to the use of dynamic framing and dramatic pose to describe a state of rest.â€™\n\nBased on Gadigal Land/Sydney, Grant Hawkes worked across various forms of photography for 20 years. His final series, made in 2016, was titled _Unexceptional Wild Flowers or I Donâ€™t Want to Photograph People Anymore_.
pigment photographic print on paper\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2025 Finalist

â€˜This photograph captures a moment of quiet reflection as my mother rests on the couch with her cigarette. After six years in Australia away from Lebanon, I returned home to surprise her. She immediately prepared my favourite meals. Exhausted from cooking all day, she came to the salon, lit her cigarette, and lay down while pots simmered on the stove. My leaving home has strengthened our relationship in ways we never experienced when we lived under the same roof. The photo is a testament to our newfound appreciation and connection.â€™\n\nAyman Kaake is a Lebanon-born Australian photo-media artist based in Naarm/Melbourne. Through his practice he explores diasporic identity, memory and the agony of exile.
archival photographic print\n\nNational Photographic Portrait Prize 2019 Finalist

â€˜Much of my work revolves around love, loss, kinship, community and belonging. I often make pictures with the people close to me, like this one of my dear friend Jackie. We were celebrating her 30th birthday; it was an exuberant night filled with love and joy. Using my camera to hold a significant moment in Jackieâ€™s journey through time, I wanted to make an intimate and celebratory picture that reflected her spirit of kindness, beauty and strength.â€™\n\nKatrin Koenning is an artist living on Wurundjeri Country in Naarm/Melbourne. Koenningâ€™s practice is anchored in the pursuit of intimacy and interconnection, and she uses the camera to both create and chronicle her community.
gelatin silver photograph on paper

â€˜Tom invited me up to Wyndham, Western Australia to photograph him and his grandad, Steve just after Christmas. This was taken in between massive afternoon downpours. The roll of Italian, medium-format cinema film jammed in my camera. I managed to salvage it and store it in a light-tight pouch away from the brutal sun and the humidity of the wet season. Two days later that pouch was opened by a curious member of the Darwin Airport security team. A week later after processing it in Sydney, it appeared that the harsh Top End had left its mark on the film.â€™\n\nT W Baker is a documentary photographer based on Dharawal Country/Helensburgh, New South Wales.
type C photograph on paper

â€˜A contagious smile to shine through these challenging times. Meet Gail Mabo, a brilliant Meriam artist from Mer Island, Torres Strait and daughter of the legendary Dr Edward Koiki Mabo. This portrait was taken during an unplanned, spontaneous session following breakfast. As Gail shared cultural and personal stories, her vibrant personality and playful energy as a natural storyteller came to life, reflected in each frame captured. A former dancer and choreographer, Gail shared her dreams of returning to the theatre. I believe this photo perfectly captures her charisma and unstoppable spirit.â€™ \n\nEnzo Frisini is a Naarm/Melbourne-based photographer.
gelatin silver photograph on paper

â€˜This work is a portrait of my partner, Brandon Mathis, inside our Los Angeles studio. I printed the work myself in the darkroom. Brandonâ€™s gaze, partially hidden by the fabric, along with the reaching hand and the rectangle of light that cuts right through him, creates a portrait that explores vulnerability, partnership dynamics and introspection. The fabric barrier becomes a metaphor for the complexities of relationships, knowing and unknowing, transparency and mystery. I also hope the viewer reflects on the delicate balance between exposure and privacy.â€™\n\nLos Angeles-based Australian photographer Luke Austin creates intimate portraits of members of the LGBTQIA+ community that reveal his subjectâ€™s individuality in a moment of disarming contact.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜The pregnant belly, a symbol of new life and transformation, is here framed between structures that represent both protection and confinement. I wanted the work to speak to the universal experience of transition, the tension between security and uncertainty, and the beauty found in the in-between spaces of lifeâ€™s unfolding journey.â€™\n\nJennie Groom is a Tarntanya/Adelaide-based photographer whose practice focuses on portraiture, feminism and social commentary.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜Mahmoud looks across the courtyard at the Flemington Housing Estate towards the building where his parents live. In a few weeks, the already mostly vacated building would be torn down to make way for new flats. On our walk across the estate, we reflected on this new reality and what it means for his family and the many other families that once called this place home.â€™\n\nBasil Abubaker is a photographer based in Naarm/Melbourne whose work explores African-Australian identity through the perspectives of young African-Australians and their communities.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜The model Nakia is a proud Yuin and Gamilaroi woman, and also my partner. We planned for this shoot for a while to ensure everything was perfect. In tribute to Nakiaâ€™s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander heritage, she wears a native floral headpiece I made for the photoshoot and a raffia skirt made by her mother. Nakia and I are both proud of our Indigenous heritage and often find it difficult to find balance between our culture and the modern world. We are both healthworkers trying to make a difference for our people.â€™\n\nSean Kinchela is a Gamilaroi and Wiradjuri man based on Yuin Country/Bodalla, New South Wales. His photography is influenced by his culture and the stories that come from the oceans, mountains, skies and land.
type C photograph on paper

â€˜Chhattisgarh is a state in central India that provides significant amounts of power to the countryâ€™s electricity grid. It is also the home of my closest friend in India and a place in which I photograph often. For the past three years Iâ€™ve dragged my friend out for early morning photo walks. On this day we met Pawan at a local pond where he had gone to bathe. He also showed us his pet turtle collection. The effects of Chhattisgarhâ€™s power success story are writ large, both upon the rapidly urbanising landscape and within its residentsâ€™ collective awareness.â€™\n\nYask Desai is a Melbourne/Naarm-based visual artist of mixed Australian and Indian heritage. He works with photography, video, archives and text to explore themes of place and collective and individual identity, as well as critiquing global political economies.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜According to Reiki philosophy, hands are the silent messengers of the soul. The loving touch of a mother is something many of us know from childhood â€“ it soothes, makes us feel safe, even heals a sore spot. A motherâ€™s caress is a miraculous remedy because touch is the first true contact with life when entering the world. The essence of touch is deep, intimate and also magical. The photograph _Hands_ captures Ojas as he holds his parentsâ€™ hands while gently resting his hand on his motherâ€™s growing belly.â€™\n\nLaura Zviedre is a Boorloo/Perth-based photographer whose documentary-style portraits capture honest and heartfelt stories.
pigment photographic print on paper

****

â€˜Every year, I ask my sons to direct a photographic portrait to give to each other as a gift. Johnny decided we must visit what he imagines to be his brother Richieâ€™s future house for a pic. Upon arrival, I was met with a beautiful slice of Australian life in all its eccentricities. This pic captures sweet nostalgia, good intentions and the overall enduring heat when wanting to wear a Christmas sweater in Australia.â€™

Mrs White aka ABBIE DAVIS is a Naarm/Melbourne-based photographer whose colour-saturated works layer pop culture and nostalgia.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜_Code Black/Riot_ is a collaboration with a group of young First Nations people in far north Queensland that interrogates a system that targets and imprisons them from the age of 10. This portrait is from the still-photo component of the larger project, made together with Vernon Ah Kee and Behrouz Boochani. Participants were invited to have their portraits taken, using a means of their own choosing to conceal their identities while making a personal statement. Some of them chose flowers or bubbles. Others a flag, mask or face paint. The three girls here chose this gesture. Many young people in this community prefer to conceal their faces in their photos to avoid being identified by the youth justice system. The result is that many families do not have photos of their children if they lose them. The project was facilitated by Youth Empowered Towards Independence in Cairns and Change the Record in Sydney.â€™\n\nHoda Afshar is a Naarm/Melbourne-based visual artist and documentary maker whose practice focuses on the intricate relationships between politics and aesthetics, knowledge and representation, visibility and violence.
type C photograph on paper

â€˜Shorty lives in one of the most rural areas of New South Wales surrounded by national parks. This is his last year before going to boarding school where he hopes to follow his love of football and meet new friends. The portrait forms part of a long-term photographic project that focuses on documenting regional agricultural life in NSW and the transition between generations of farmers.â€™\n\nLuke David Kellett lives and works in Newcastle, NSW, on the Country of the Awabakal and Worimi peoples. His documentary photographs capture different parts of Australian life.

labels.title: Anna (Home for a Time)
labels.subtitle: (Nur) Aishah Kenton and Anna Jourdant
labels.medium: inkjet photographic print, mixed media and textiles

text.content: inkjet photographic print, mixed media and textiles

â€˜Sharehouse living has long been a rite of passage for young Australians. Once considered an important social conduit between adolescence and adulthood, it is now a more permanent housing solution for many Australians. Anna lives in a sharehouse in Meanjin/Brisbane, Queensland. â€œYou learn a lot about yourself and what you value living in a sharehouse,â€ Anna says. Annaâ€™s creative spirit inspired this mixed-media, collaborative portrait and she added the hand-colouring and embroidery. I knew any representation of her would need to be more than just a simple photo.â€™\n\n(Nur) Aishah Kenton is a Singapore-born, Malay artist based in Naarm/Melbourne who uses photography, installation and collaborative methods to weave together personal histories and broader narratives. For this portrait they have collaborated with Anna Jourdant, a Meanjin/Brisbane-based artist who works with stained glass, textiles and found objects.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜Sonny Jane is a queer, non-binary, disabled and neurodivergent advocate and writer, and defier of systems. â€œSince I was young, I was in and out of the mental health system where I was labelled as defiant, naughty and stubborn. My â€˜defiantâ€™ tattoo is a commitment to resist systems that pathologise our minds, bodies and queerness. My rainbow freckle tattoos are about wearing my personality and queerness on my face. When people look at me, theyâ€™re going to see who I am.â€ My work is often playful, but also aims to challenge in its own unexpected ways.â€™\n\nBri Hammond is an artist living and working on Kaurna land in Tarntanya/Adelaide. Hammond creates work that blends authentic emotion with wry observation to highlight the idiosyncrasies of people and places.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜This photograph captures a moment of quiet reflection as my mother rests on the couch with her cigarette. After six years in Australia away from Lebanon, I returned home to surprise her. She immediately prepared my favourite meals. Exhausted from cooking all day, she came to the salon, lit her cigarette, and lay down while pots simmered on the stove. My leaving home has strengthened our relationship in ways we never experienced when we lived under the same roof. The photo is a testament to our newfound appreciation and connection.â€™\n\nAyman Kaake is a Lebanon-born Australian photo-media artist based in Naarm/Melbourne. Through contemplative portraiture Kaake explores diasporic melancholy and the agony of exile.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜This work explores themes of renewal, identity and belonging. Wrapped in a golden emergency blanket and resting on a tumbled stone, my mother represents strength and adaptability, finding hope through her migration story. The golden blanket, a symbol of safety and care, contrasts with the grounding presence of the stone. Together, they reflect the tension between aspiration, humility, fragility and resilience. My practice explores the in-betweenness of identity, honouring my motherâ€™s experience while encouraging viewers to reflect on their own connections to migration, home and the longing for belonging.â€™\n\nSherry Quiambao is an Australian-Filipino multidisciplinary artist based in Boorloo/Perth, Western Australia. Quiambaoâ€™s practice draws from personal and cultural narratives to question material culture and its role in shaping belonging and self-image.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜I am drawn in by the powers and potentials for in/visibility in portraiture, for playful evasion, for the performance of dis/appearing acts in which I pass before the camera un/seen. My interest in portraiture lies in the way artists â€“ and I think queer artists in particular are quite attuned to this â€“ can pervert the conditions of the portrait by toying with or complicating their own visibility. I am drawn toward portraiture that redistributes power toward the subject in interesting ways, allowing the subject to be the one who determines the ways, as well as the extent to which, they are seen by both camera and viewer.â€™\n\nGerwyn Davies is a queer artist based on Gadigal land/Sydney who works across photography, textile and costume. Davies takes a performative approach to photographic portraiture, exploring self-representation, camp aesthetics and kitsch Australiana.
type C photograph on paper

â€˜Thom Roberts at home in what he calls â€œDonkey Big Bird Stationâ€, also known as Pennant Hills. I work with the artist Thom Roberts at Studio A and wanted to photograph him in his home environment. Thom sees and identifies his world and community through the lens of popular culture and the constructed world. For Thom, humans can be skyscrapers, the cityâ€™s infrastructure are his friends, and he is a CountryLink Express train. His perspective challenges the everyday humdrum of day-to-day life in this crazy world.â€™\n\nTanja Bruckner is a photographer based on Gadigal land/Sydney whose imagery aims to disrupt homogenous narratives and encourage inclusivity. Bruckner is driven by a strong focus on social justice and womenâ€™s and LGBTQIA+ rights. Studio A is a supported studio that creates professional pathways for artists with lived experience of intellectual disability.
type C photograph on paper

â€˜Oaklanâ€™s story is extraordinary. Diagnosed with a rare disease affecting fewer than 500 boys worldwide, heâ€™s faced more in his young life than most could imagine. At four, he underwent a bone marrow transplant, losing his hair to chemo â€“ but then his mighty mullet was born. His journey includes countless life-saving surgeries, including a full spinal fusion last year, where his surgeon ensured his iconic hairstyle stayed intact. Though his school recently made him cut the mullet, his spirit remains unshaken. Oaklan is a walking miracle and a true Aussie legend.â€™ \n\nKristian Taylor-Wood is a London-born photographer, director and writer based on Gadigal land/Sydney whose portraits focus on unconventional and thought-provoking storytelling.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜Amazine and her father, Amaziah Club, took part in a menâ€™s ceremony in Ampilatwatja, on the Alyawarre homelands, 325km northeast of Alice Springs. This image is from the series _Tea and Sugar_, which documents families involved in the landmark Stolen Wages class action against the Commonwealth Government in 2024. The lawsuit sought justice for the thousands of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples who worked on Northern Territory cattle stations between 1933 and 1971, receiving little or no wages â€“ only â€œtea and sugarâ€. Amazine and Amaziah are descendants of Banjo Morton, who led the original protest for fair wages and recognition.â€™\n\nPaul Blackmore is a photojournalist based in Cavanbah/Byron Bay, New South Wales who covers social and political issues in Australia and internationally. His works explore the relationships between humanity and the extraordinary forces that shape our lives.

labels.title: You cannot leave it behind, for it will follow you
labels.subtitle: Georgia Wilde

text.content: pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜When I was younger, I used to feel that travel provided a temporary escape from life. I took this self portrait when I spent a week in tropical Ubud, Bali. It captures how it felt to try, and fail, at outrunning problems from home. It is unnatural to force the body to relax, and to let that discomfort be seen.â€™\n\nBased on Gadigal land/Sydney, Georgia Wilde works in video art, installation and mixed media. Her practice explores personal mythology, youth, womanhood and the body, and considers the way these themes interact with broader political and cultural landscapes.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜I made this photograph with Gamilaraay musician Thelma Plum on Wilyakali Country last winter. The image was shot using a Rolleicord camera on the Mundi Mundi Plains near the outback town of Broken Hill, where I live. We spent three days photographing throughout the far west New South Wales region, making a series of photographs for Thelmaâ€™s album _Iâ€™m Sorry, Now Say It Back_.â€™\n\nEm Jensen lives and works on Wilyakali Country in Broken Hill, NSW. Her practice explores themes of nostalgia, fringe subcultures and the Australian character, with a focus on sharing the stories of people in regional and remote parts of the country.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜As part of my series _Deep Heat_, I took this portrait â€œwithâ€ Antony Sinni, a non-binary friend/artist/icon (they/them) on Larrakia Land, Garramilla/Darwin. I highlight â€œwithâ€ because making an image like this is both individual and deeply collaborative. Entangled as a singular organism, experiencing what it is to be within a moment of vulnerability, connected by the sand, sky and the lens. This image sums up the series well, using photography to explore my complex relationship with gender and masculinity. Creating an opportunity for healing and evolution.â€™\n\nBased in Rubibi/Broome, Western Australia, multidisciplinary artist Matt Sav works across photography and film to investigate the intersection of gender, ecology, intimacy and isolation.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜Black Swan Theory originates from Europeans believing only white swans existed until they â€œvisitedâ€ Western Australia in 1697, shocked to discover something so rare and beautiful as a Black Swan. The denial of the Maali/Black Swan serves as a greater metaphor for the failure of Europeans to acknowledge the beauty and sovereignty of First Nations peoples and their connection to this land, and the denial of queer people throughout history. This portrait is a tribute to WA, where Will grew up, and honours Garrettâ€™s First Nations heritage, two queer swans floating in the romantic haze of a disco-enthused lake.â€™\n\nWill Huxley and Garrett Huxley are Naarm/Melbourne-based collaborative performance and visual artists. The Huxleysâ€™ performances traverse the classifications of costume, film and recording in what they describe as a visual assault of sparkle, surrealism and the absurd.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜This image of Philomela is from _Lest We Forget_, a series of large photographic light paintings that recreate scenes from Greco-Roman mythology that depict rape. The work focuses on re-codifying mythological womenâ€™s experiences of rape to centre the victim-survivor. Through feminist intervention the work investigates the origins of the stories, alters perspective and challenges established gendered tropes.â€™\n\nDida Sundet is an interdisciplinary artist from Norway, based in Boorloo/Perth, who works with the photographic technique that she terms light painting, using long exposures to â€˜paintâ€™ with light. Her practice focuses on the connections between ancient mythology, traditional gender stereotypes and current sociopolitical debates around menâ€™s violence towards women.
pigment print on HahnemÃ¼hle cotton rag satin paper

â€˜Ghyslaine Gau appears here as both subject and fragment. Born in Marseille to Martinican parents and raised in the suburbs of Paris, she is a dancer, performer and part of the collective Wusinsans with Constanza Mendoza and I. Inspired by Ã‰douard Glissantâ€™s concept of the abyss, this portrait â€“ shot on film â€“ gestures toward the unknown between self and other. It reflects the impossibility of fully capturing or knowing another, embracing relationality and absence. Resisting conventional portraiture, it offers a glimpse into a moment that remains incomplete, echoing the limits of language and perception.â€™\n\nShoufay Derz is an interdisciplinary artist working on Gadigal land/Sydney. Drawing on poetic and philosophical frameworks, her practice explores themes of transformation, absence and shared uncertainties.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜Itâ€™s a common feeling among the queer community â€“ the deep desire to run into the forest, strip naked and just be â€œflaming faggotsâ€. To reclaim the words that they call us and start our own rituals. For _FAGGOT MAGIC BONFIRE_, we wanted to embody this feeling. Informed by our shared queer experiences and an agreement to â€œmake it super witchyâ€, we stoked the fire and created all our effects in-camera. Happy accidents and unexpected shapes form the final image, calling upon ancient queer magics that emerged from primordial body ooze, still sparkling and glistening long after we return to gay little dust.â€™\n\nJeff Andersen Jnr. is a Naarm/Melbourne-based photographer and filmmaker. His photographs explore movement, shape and shadow with themes of queer joy, amplifying mood through lighting and cinematic haze.
type C photograph & photogram on paper

â€˜When I visited Aida while she was living in Manila, Philippines, I made a portrait using a box camera built by local photographers Krystine Antonio, Jesed Moreno and Marion. Aida and I decorated the paper negative with her stickers, and then I rephotographed it. In November, Aida moved to Tarntanya/Adelaide to be with family, especially her sister who was about to have a baby. During this time I reshot the print, adding a Baby Taz sticker Aida sent me years ago, and a jelly centipede on the paper as a photogram.â€™\n\nTarntanya/Adelaide-based artist Emmaline Zanelli creates constructed compositions that amplify the expressive power of objects and images. Her portraits explore the relationship between photography, memory and identity.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜17-year resident John Patmore is one of 32 battlers living in four old boarding houses in Sydneyâ€™s Paddington. â€œI thought Iâ€™d be able to live here â€™til the day I die after my super started to run out. But now â€¦ This place is going to close on January 31, and weâ€™re all being kicked out. Iâ€™ve got nowhere to go. Itâ€™s just so overwhelming.â€ It is a classic battle between a developer who wants to push residents out for profit and a vulnerable community who have called this boarding house home for many years. Where do they go now?â€™ \n\nDion Georgopoulos is a multimedia journalist and filmmaker based on Gadigal land/Sydney who shares his passion for visual storytelling across photography and video.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜Dame Stan Munro, aged 84, is arguably Australiaâ€™s oldest performing drag queen. Born in Wales, he made his debut as a child actor/performer before touring the United Kingdom, Ireland and Germany. In 1963, Stan migrated to Australia as a â€œTen Pound Pomâ€ where he discovered drag after joining the Sydney review show, _Les Girls_. He became their star performer and compere and in the 1970s continued with Melbourne _Les Girls_. After meeting him at the local gym in Kyogle, New South Wales, where he lives, I was compelled to photograph him. His portrait forms part of a growing body of portraits in rural Kyogle.â€™\n\nJodie Harris is a Yamatji and Wadjari photographer working on Bundjalung Country in northern New South Wales. Her experimental practice crosses the genres of environmental portraiture and social documentary.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜This photo captures the intimate chaos of a life lived in one space, my childhood bedroom, for 34 years. Surrounded by a tapestry of trinkets and the quiet clutter of everyday life, my self portrait reflects the intersection of nostalgia and the present. The disorder becomes a tangible reminder of time passing, of a personal history that clings to the space, the room itself as much a part of my identity as the person within it.â€™\n\nTom Zust is a Slovenian-Australian artist and photographer who lives and works on the land of the Darug people in Western Sydney. Zust is engaged in the relationship between identity, artifice and photographic depiction.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜_Lurking_ is a self portrait created at the Leveld Kunstnartun art residency in rural Norway. The photograph features custom-made leather harnesses I made during the residency. Set against the rural backdrop, the urban leather contrasts with the weathered wood, symbolising the tension between isolation and resilience often present in queer experiences. The work invites viewers to contemplate queerness as both an inner journey and an ongoing dialogue with the world around us.â€™\n\nDerek Sargent is a Tarntanya/Adelaide-based artist whose practice includes moving image, sculpture, installation and photography. His work investigates themes of sexual identity and authenticity and questions dominant histories and narratives.
type C photograph on paper

â€˜This is a portrait of Kyanne, who enjoys fishing, spending afternoons with family, and hopes to work with children in the future. The photograph was taken at the 2024 NAIDOC Ball, which fosters confidence, belief, courage and hope among the youth of Aurukun. Aurukun is home to five main spiritual clan groups: Apalech, Winchanam, Wanam, Chara and Puutch.â€™ \n\nDavid Prichard is a photographer based on Bundjalung Country/Byron Bay whose portraits create space for the subject to command the frame.
tintype, Chromaluxe metal print

â€˜Rav, depicted here, is a proud Indian trans man, born in Singapore, who moved to Australia for love and queer community. â€œIt took me a long time to come to terms with my queer and trans identity while shutting down the voices in my head that say Indians canâ€™t be queer or trans and that itâ€™s a whitewashed thing. Itâ€™s innate for me. I was born this way and to be able to celebrate my identity along with my culture is my biggest achievement.â€â€™\n\nPrue Hazelgrove is a Queer Canberra-based artist living on unceded Ngunnawal Country who specialises in the 19th-century wet plate collodion process. The historical significance of this medium enables them to represent stories erased from the narrative.
wet plate collodion tintype

â€˜Wet plate collodion was the pre-eminent photographic technology of the 1860s. The images exist as highlights of pure silver metal on a black background. The process is arcane, alchemical and potentially explosive. Fickle too, as a tiny deviation in the workflow may result in the complete absence of emulsion. Muni kindly sat for a portrait in my Pomona studio. We relinquished our control to the process, and it imposed its will upon us. In our flaws we find our greatest strength.â€™\n\nRaoul Slater is a photographer from Pomona on the land of the Kabi Kabi/Gubbi Gubbi peoples on Queenslandâ€™s Sunshine Coast. He has recently been working in the medium of wet plate collodion.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜This is a very special place for me and my family at the river Langi. Being on Country means reconnecting with nature and its healing powers. My Country and family are recurring subjects in my work. The child in the picture is Violet, my niece, who is about to throw the net. Children learn from the age of five how to handle a fishing net. The picture is a representation of belonging to Country and Violet personifies the pride that goes with belonging, skills, knowing about your heritage and living within your culture.â€™\n\nNyikina, Yawuru, Ngul Ngul and Ngarinyin photographer Mary-Lou Orliyarli Divilli was born in Derby, Western Australia. She is inspired by older generations and their depth of cultural knowledge expressed through stories and traditional song.
gelatin silver photograph on paper

â€˜Intimacy can be so much more than the popular definition. This photo depicts Kayleb painting up his partner Britney in a design that speaks of love and loss. Britney and Kayleb are both incredible cultural dancers and would later that evening dance together to further display the depth of love and loss that they have experienced. Culture is a powerful healer. Waagan Galga Corroboree, Wonnarua Country, November 2024.â€™ \n\nBiripi and Dhungutti photographer Marcus Rowsell lives on Worimi Country in Forster, New South Wales. He shoots primarily in black-and-white 35mm film, a deliberate choice to strip away complexity and focus on the raw beauty of everyday moments.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜Zev and Nick met 15 years ago and have been together for eight years. Their relationship developed over time and they now share a home and often a bed. They have plans for the future. Zev is queer and seven months into their relationship began medically transitioning. Nick also has a girlfriend and they have been going out for three years. Zev was not in any other relationship at the time of the portrait. Zev and Nickâ€™s relationship is non-monogamous and they love each other.â€™\n\nHilary Wardhaugh is a photographer, artist and activist based on Ngunnawal and Ngambri land in Canberra whose practice explores humanity and the environment through a feminist lens.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜This photograph was made in the home of Sarah and Dylan, five months after the sudden passing of their late husband and father, Norman. Norman was my GP who helped me with lifesaving medication through suicidal depression. Following his death I temporarily moved into Sarah and Dylanâ€™s apartment to help support them. I created this image using a bedside lamp held in my hand and a subtle front swing. Sarah, an ex-sex worker and a lifelong photographic artist, has been a champion of mine since the beginning of my photographic journey back in 2015.â€™\n\nRyan Dandelion is a portrait artist based on Bundjalung land/Lismore working with analogue photography and printing techniques. Dandelionâ€™s practice explores themes of vulnerability, sexuality, and the relationship between photographer and subject.
pigment photographic print on paper

â€˜â€œQueer people must literally construct the houses they will be born intoâ€ â€“ Nayland Blake. I return to ideas about home and queerness regularly in my work. Home is a place Iâ€™ve run from most of my life; home is a place Iâ€™ve needed to find. On a recent trip interstate, I visited my friend Riley and his partner James. Seeing them so at ease with each other in their home reminded me of the peace Iâ€™ve found at home with my partner. In this shallow focus close-up, Riley frames James in an over-the-shoulder embrace.â€™\n\nTorrey Bruinstroop is a photographer and writer who lives in Magandjin/Brisbane. Bruinstroop combines analogue in-camera techniques with minimal digital editing to create images that are rooted in the aesthetics of 20th-century queer photographers such as David Wojnarowicz, George Platt Lynes and Peter Hujar.
